## 37th pass: full refutation of the 35th pass's `transmute`/aliasing hypothesis -- `deallocate`'s call chain NEVER actually touches the page lists in THIS version of the crate, so there is no live second `&mut P` to alias against. This entire line of investigation is now closed.

Traced `deallocate`'s complete call chain: `SCAllocator::deallocate` (`sc.rs:305-326`) calls `slab_page.deallocate(ptr, new_layout)` (line 323) and does nothing else with `slab_page`. `ObjectPage::deallocate` (`pages.rs:205-222`) -- what that call actually invokes -- takes `&self` and does exactly one thing: clears a single bit in the page's own internal bitfield (`self.bitfield().clear_bit(idx)`, line 220). **It never touches `self.slabs`/`self.empty_slabs`/`self.full_slabs` at all.** The crate's own doc comment describing list-migration on deallocation ("we might move a page from full_slabs to slabs or from slabs to empty_slabs after we deallocated an object", `sc.rs:42-43`) describes INTENDED future behavior that is not actually implemented in this checked-out revision -- independently confirmed by this project's own `SafeZoneAllocator::dealloc` (`litebox/src/mm/allocator.rs:228`) carrying its own `// TODO: An proper reclamation strategy could be implemented here to release empty pages back from the ZoneAllocator to the buddy allocator` comment, i.e. this project's own author already knows/documents that page reclamation-on-free isn't wired up yet.

**With no list access inside `deallocate` at all, the `transmute`d `&mut P` in `deallocate` can never alias against any reference `allocate`'s list-walking code holds** (there is nothing for it to alias against during a deallocate call) -- the 35th pass's proposed mechanism is fully refuted, not merely weakened. The crate's own `// TODO: The linked list will have another &mut reference` comment (`sc.rs:319`) most likely describes a FUTURE concern the author anticipated for when reclamation IS implemented, not a currently-live bug in the code as it exists in this exact pinned revision (`19480b2e82704210abafe575fb9699184c1be110`).

**This closes out the `slabmalloc`-internal-unsoundness investigative thread (passes 15-16, 33, 35-37) without a confirmed fix** -- extensive reading of the actual vendored source across multiple passes has not found a genuine bug in the crate's own logic for this specific, pinned revision. The `SLAB_ALLOC`-address-resolving fault captures (33rd pass) remain real and unexplained, but are now understood NOT to originate from this specific aliasing concern. Given how many individually-plausible mechanisms this investigation has proposed and then refuted upon closer reading (TF/hardware-breakpoint leak, SuspendThread lock-abandonment, create_pages/op TOCTOU-reachability, tar_no_std torn reads, and now this transmute-aliasing theory), the project's own code and its dependencies have now had an extraordinarily thorough audit with no confirmed logic bug found anywhere -- strengthening the case that the actual mechanism is either a genuine Windows-OS-level nondeterminism (page commit/TLB/cache timing under this project's specific thread-suspend patterns) or a bug in a part of the codebase this investigation has not yet examined (the buddy allocator, `LockedHeapWithRescue`, or the interaction between the two allocators' own address-range partitioning).

## 35th pass: FOUND A REAL, UPSTREAM-ACKNOWLEDGED UNSOUNDNESS in the vendored `slabmalloc` crate itself -- `SCAllocator::deallocate` conjures a `&mut P` reference via `transmute` from a raw address while the SAME page is simultaneously reachable through the allocator's own intrusive linked lists, with the crate's OWN source comment admitting this is an unresolved TODO. This is likely the actual root cause, independent of any lock/thread-safety bug in this project's own code.

Read the vendored `slabmalloc` git dependency's source directly (`C:\Users\user\.cargo\git\checkouts\rust-slabmalloc-7c04d7ad33e8d90d\19480b2\src\sc.rs`). Noted `SCAllocator::allocate` takes `&mut self` (line 251) but `SCAllocator::deallocate` takes only `&self` (line 305) -- verified this is NOT a locking bug in THIS project's own code (`litebox/src/mm/allocator.rs:215-227`'s `SafeZoneAllocator::dealloc` correctly calls `self.slab_allocator.lock().deallocate(...)`, going through the SAME `SpinMutex` as `alloc` every time, so both calls ARE mutually exclusive at the project's own usage layer).

**The real problem is INSIDE `deallocate`'s own implementation** (`sc.rs:316-325`): `let slab_page = unsafe { mem::transmute::<VAddr, &'a mut P>(page) };` -- conjuring a live `&'a mut P` (mutable reference to the object page) directly from a raw virtual address via `transmute`, with the function's OWN preceding source comment (line 319) reading verbatim: **"TODO: The linked list will have another &mut reference"** -- i.e. the crate's own author has already identified, in a code comment, that this SAME page object is simultaneously reachable as a live node inside `self.empty_slabs`/`self.slabs`/`self.full_slabs` (the intrusive `PageList<P>` structures `allocate`'s own code walks using ITS OWN mutable references), meaning `deallocate` can create a SECOND, ALIASING `&mut P` to memory another `&mut P` already (potentially) references -- a direct violation of Rust's aliasing model (`&mut` references must be provably exclusive; LLVM is permitted to assume this for optimization purposes), independent of any external lock. **A mutex serializes WHEN the two `&mut` references are CREATED/USED in program order, but does not prevent the compiler from having already generated code that assumes non-aliasing based on the (violated) type-level guarantee** -- this is exactly the class of bug that can produce silent, seemingly-nondeterministic memory corruption that gets WORSE under specific optimization levels/inlining decisions (release-only, exactly matching this whole session's own repeatedly-confirmed observation that this bug never reproduces in a debug build) and is extremely sensitive to subtle timing/scheduling differences (matching every diagnostic-masks-the-bug observation this entire investigation has made).

**This is now the single most concrete, well-evidenced, and plausible root cause identified in this entire multi-session investigation** -- not a bug in this project's own Rust code (every subsystem this session read in `litebox`/`litebox_shim_linux`/`litebox_platform_windows_userland` has checked out as correct), but a genuine, author-acknowledged soundness gap in the third-party `slabmalloc` crate's own `deallocate` path, exactly the kind of UB that (a) requires nothing more than ordinary concurrent allocate/deallocate pressure to trigger (explaining the fork-count threshold, 34th pass -- more concurrent threads means more chances for the compiler's aliasing-based optimizations to actually misbehave in a way that's observable), (b) is binary-independent (34th pass -- `/bin/true` crashes just as well as `labwc`, since ANY guest process doing ANY allocation contributes to the same shared corruption risk), and (c) explains why static review of every OTHER subsystem this session checked kept coming back clean -- the bug was never in this project's own code to find.

**Concrete, well-scoped, high-confidence next step for a future session**: patch the local `slabmalloc` checkout (already fetchable/editable at the path above; wire in via a `[patch]` section in `litebox/Cargo.toml`, e.g. `[patch."https://github.com/gz/rust-slabmalloc.git"]` pointing at a local path) to fix this specific unsoundness -- the correct fix is almost certainly to make `deallocate` take `&mut self` (matching `allocate`), removing the need for the `transmute`-conjured second `&mut P` entirely by routing the deallocation through the SAME already-`&mut`-borrowed linked-list traversal `allocate` uses, OR (if `&mut self` is infeasible for API reasons) to use `UnsafeCell`-based interior mutability consistently and genuinely soundly (a `*mut P` raw pointer with actual raw-pointer field access, never materializing a second live `&mut P` reference at all) rather than `transmute`ing into a reference. Given `deallocate` is only ever called from `SafeZoneAllocator::dealloc`, which ALREADY holds `self.slab_allocator.lock()` for the whole call, changing `deallocate`'s signature to `&mut self` should be a purely mechanical, safe, zero-behavior-change fix at this project's own call site -- test it against the new minimal N=10-fork `/bin/true` repro (34th pass) for fast, high-confidence verification once made.

This crashed with the IDENTICAL fault chain as the GUI repro: first fault `write_u8_fallible+0x6` (`rva=0x6770a6`, confirmed for the Nth time as the true, universal first fault), secondary fault at `rva=0x77aa` (`tar_no_std::TarFormatNumber::as_number`'s address -- the SAME exact address the 29th pass captured under the full GUI/labwc-autostart repro, now reproduced under a completely unrelated, much simpler scenario).

**This is the single most important finding of the entire investigation**: the crash has NOTHING to do with labwc's compositor logic, DRM/KMS, weston, seatd, or `--gui` presentation at all -- it is a pure, generic fork()+execve() concurrency bug in litebox's own process/memory-management machinery, triggered by simply launching enough concurrent child processes in a short window. `labwc --version` was chosen somewhat arbitrarily (as a large, real ELF binary happening to be present) -- the crash's dependence on WHICH binary is executed, or whether it's genuinely about "how many forks" vs. "how much concurrent memory-management work", is now the most valuable next question, and one this minimal repro makes CHEAP AND FAST to answer (a `labwc --version` invocation exits almost instantly, unlike the multi-second GUI startup every previous capture required).

**Concrete, immediately actionable next steps for a future session, now with a MUCH faster iteration loop**: (1) sweep the fork COUNT (try 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20 concurrent forks of the same command) to find the minimum count that reliably triggers the crash -- this directly tests whether "3 forks" (this project's own long-standing folklore threshold, referenced throughout this session's memory/AGENTS.md history) is still the real threshold, or whether it's actually about a much higher concurrency level that GUI startup's own thread count coincidentally reaches; (2) try substituting a SMALL, trivial static binary (`/bin/true`, `/bin/echo`) in place of `labwc` for the same fork-count sweep, to test whether the crash needs a LARGE binary (many ELF segments, more BSS zero-fill calls) or reproduces even for a tiny one -- directly testing whether segment COUNT/SIZE is a factor; (3) once a minimal, fast, reliable trigger is found, this becomes an ideal target for either a genuinely non-perturbing diagnostic (fast iteration means even a moderately-heavy one is now affordable) or for finally bisecting exactly which of the N concurrent forks' own `ElfParsedFile::load` call is the one that faults, and correlating it with what the OTHER N-1 concurrent forks were doing at that exact moment.

The `pm()` accessor is itself mutex-guarded, so no torn/partial-swap state is observable either. There is no window where a live, running parent could touch the same `Vmem` the child's own execve mapping work is using.

## 26th pass: resolved the 25th pass's own open question immediately -- the lock-leak-via-interrupt hypothesis is REFUTED. `Vmem`-mutating code (syscall handlers like `sys_mmap`) always runs with `is_in_guest=false`, so `ThreadHandle::interrupt`'s existing early-return (confirmed correct behavior, 17th pass) already protects every `self.vmem.write()` critical section from being suspended-and-abandoned.

`is_in_guest` is cleared at the very start of `syscall_callback` (the naked-asm trampoline every guest syscall instruction jumps into, `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs` ~line 2293-2294, `mov BYTE PTR [r11 + IS_IN_GUEST], 0`, read in full multiple times earlier this session) and only set back to `true` when control actually returns to guest code. All of `sys_mmap`/`sys_munmap`/`Vmem::create_pages`/`remove_pages`/etc. run entirely as HOST Rust code reached FROM that trampoline, strictly between the clear and the eventual guest-resume -- meaning `target_tls.is_in_guest.get()` is ALWAYS `false` for a thread caught mid-`Vmem`-mutation. `ThreadHandle::interrupt` (`lib.rs:3775-3779`, quoted in full in the 17th pass) takes its early-return path (`if !target_tls.is_in_guest.get() { return; }`) for exactly this case -- it sets the interrupt flag and resumes the thread immediately, WITHOUT ever redirecting `rip`/injecting `interrupt_callback`. **This means a thread suspended mid-`Vmem`-mutation is never abandoned mid-critical-section by `interrupt()`** -- it gets its flag set and continues running normally, checking the flag at its own next natural opportunity (a syscall return, per the surrounding code's own design). The 25th pass's lock-leak hypothesis is therefore REFUTED, symmetric with the (also refuted) TF/hardware-breakpoint hypothesis from passes 16-17 -- both assumed `interrupt()` does something unsafe to a thread caught in host code, and both times the actual code turned out to already correctly special-case exactly that scenario.

**Updated overall assessment after 26 passes**: this session has now individually verified as CORRECT (not buggy) essentially every major subsystem touching this crash's own call chain -- `fork_verify`'s TF arm/disarm symmetry (8th/17th), `ThreadHandle::interrupt`'s guest-vs-host suspend handling (17th/26th, twice now), the `create_pages`/`op` mmap-then-populate sequencing being provably synchronous in the SINGLE-threaded sense (23rd), ELF program-header parsing arithmetic (21st) and observed values (22nd), and `kill_other_threads`'s own thread-count-based completion signal (26th, this pass, now cleared). The one STRUCTURALLY REAL but not-yet-confirmed-reachable finding remains the 24th pass's `create_pages`/`op` unlocked window itself (a genuine TOCTOU IF some other actor can reach the same `Vmem`, which `kill_other_threads`/`detach_pm_for_vfork_execve` appear to exclude for the ordinary same-process/vfork cases, but were not exhaustively verified beyond the top-level read already done). Given how many individually-plausible hypotheses have now been tested and refuted with real, cited evidence, the remaining bug is likely either: (a) a genuinely rare, hard-to-reach edge case in one of the "already verified correct" paths that a top-level read doesn't surface (e.g. an error path, a specific flag combination, or a currently-unconsidered interaction between two independently-correct pieces), or (b) something entirely outside this specific call chain that this session's evidence (the ring-buffer-captured true-first-fault, `write_u8_fallible` inside `ElfParsedFile::load`) has correctly localized the SYMPTOM to, but whose actual CAUSE lies further upstream in a part of the codebase not yet examined at all this session.

## 25th pass: read `kill_other_threads()`'s full implementation -- found a real gap that plausibly explains the HANG behavior (not necessarily the crash): it waits for `nr_threads == 1`, but `interrupt()` merely SIGNALS a sibling thread to exit via `SuspendThread`+redirect, with no guarantee the sibling wasn't suspended WHILE HOLDING `vmem`'s write lock, in which case that lock is never released and this thread's own later `create_pages` call deadlocks forever.

`kill_other_threads()` (`litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/process.rs:867-914`): marks every sibling thread `is_exiting`, calls `thread.interrupt()` on each (the SAME `SuspendThread`/`SetThreadContext`-redirect mechanism examined in depth across passes 8/16/17 for a DIFFERENT hazard), then loops waiting for `nr_threads.underlying_atomic() == 1` (i.e. waits for the COUNT to drop, via each thread's own exit path presumably decrementing it and calling `.block()`'s wake).

**The gap**: `interrupt()` redirects a suspended thread's `rip` to jump to `interrupt_callback` on its NEXT resume -- but does nothing to un-wind or release any Rust-level lock (like `vmem`'s `RwLock`) the thread might currently hold at the exact instruction it was suspended at. If a sibling thread is caught by `SuspendThread` WHILE INSIDE a `self.vmem.write()`-guarded critical section (e.g. its own `mmap`/`munmap`/`remove_pages` call, entirely plausible given `seatd`/labwc's own concurrent thread activity), redirecting its `rip` to `interrupt_callback` means it NEVER returns to the code that would have called `RwLock::write`'s drop/unlock -- **that lock is now held forever by a thread that has jumped away from the code holding it**, an genuine and permanent lock leak. `kill_other_threads()`'s own wait loop only checks the thread COUNT, not lock state, so it can complete successfully (`nr_threads == 1`) while `self.vmem` remains permanently write-locked by the now-defunct former holder.

**This would produce exactly a HANG, not a crash**: any LATER call in the newly-execve'ing thread that needs `self.vmem.write()` (e.g. `create_pages` for the new ELF's own segments, or `release_memory`'s own lock acquisition just before that) would block forever trying to acquire an already-and-permanently-held lock. **This is a strong, independent, and highly plausible explanation for the dominant "hang at the same 77-line point" behavior this session has observed increasingly often** (11th, 18th-20th passes) as a DISTINCT failure mode from the (also real, separately investigated) `write_u8_fallible` crash -- the two may be two different symptoms of related timing pressure, or entirely independent bugs that happen to manifest at the same point in the startup sequence.

**Not yet fixed this pass** (time-boxed): confirming this requires either (a) a live capture at the exact moment of a hang showing a thread stuck waiting on `self.vmem`'s `RwLock` specifically (not yet directly observed -- prior hang captures, 11th/18th passes, showed threads blocked on `sys_wait4`/`pty_ioctl` futexes, not a `vmem` lock acquisition site by name, though a blocked `RwLock::write()` call might not show a distinctive symbol in a heuristic stack walk), or (b) reading `ThreadHandle::interrupt`'s exact redirect mechanism once more specifically to determine whether it ONLY ever redirects a thread that is `is_in_guest` (host-code threads take the early-return path per the 17th pass's own finding) -- if `vmem`-holding code only ever runs as HOST code (never marked `is_in_guest`), then `interrupt()`'s existing `if !target_tls.is_in_guest.get() { return; }` early-return (confirmed correct behavior, 17th pass) would ALREADY protect against this exact scenario, since a thread suspended while doing host-side `Vmem` work would take that safe fast path and just get its interrupt flag set, resuming normally to finish its own critical section -- which would fully REFUTE this pass's own hypothesis. This distinction (is `Vmem`-mutating code ever reachable while `is_in_guest` is true?) is the single most valuable thing for a future session to resolve first, before assuming this lock-leak theory is correct.

## 24th pass: found and precisely cited a REAL structural TOCTOU (`create_pages` drops its `vmem` write lock before calling `op`, which is where the crashing `write_u8_fallible` write happens) via a dispatched workflow audit -- but traced the specific `execve` call path and found the two obvious concurrent actors (other same-process threads, a still-attached vfork parent) already appear to be excluded by existing guards, so this race's reachability for THIS specific crash remains unconfirmed; did NOT implement a fix given the real risk of introducing a deadlock instead.

A parallel workflow dispatch (one repro run + one static-audit agent) confirmed: `PageManager::create_pages` (`litebox/src/mm/mod.rs:846-883`) acquires `self.vmem.write()` only for the `vmem.create_pages(...)` call itself (858-861), then EXPLICITLY DROPS the lock (the comment at line 863 says why: `op` -- the caller-supplied initialization closure -- "may trigger page fault handler which requires write lock to `vmem`", so holding it across `op` would self-deadlock) before calling `op(addr)` at line 864. For the ELF loader's BSS zero-fill path, `op` IS the closure that eventually calls `write_at_offset`/`write_u8_fallible` (`litebox_common_linux/src/loader.rs`'s `AccessMemory::zero`, confirmed call chain from the 21st pass). The audit further confirmed `write_at_offset`'s `NoValidation::validate` (`litebox/src/platform/common_providers/userspace_pointers.rs:81-88`) is a pure no-op (`Some(ptr)` unconditionally) -- there is genuinely no bounds/mapping check defending this specific write at all; it relies entirely on the CPU fault + exception-table recovery mechanism, which (per every earlier pass) sometimes fails to engage.

**This is a real, structurally-confirmed unlocked window**: between `create_pages` returning the new mapping's address and `op` finishing its writes into it, ANY OTHER CODE PATH that can acquire `self.vmem.write()` (e.g. `remove_pages` at line 1286, `release_memory`, a `brk` shrink) and target the SAME address range would corrupt/unmap the mapping mid-write, with no defense on the write side.

**However, tracing the SPECIFIC `sys_execve` call path that leads to the crashing `ElfParsedFile::load` call** (`litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/process.rs`, `sys_execve`, ~line 4155-4230) found that the two most obvious concurrent-actor candidates both appear to be excluded BEFORE the new ELF's own mapping/zero-fill work begins: (1) `self.kill_other_threads()` (line 4183) runs and waits for every OTHER thread of THIS SAME guest process to fully exit before any new-ELF mapping work starts -- so a same-process sibling thread cannot be the racing actor; (2) `self.process().detach_pm_for_vfork_execve(...)` (line 4198) runs before `release_memory`/the new ELF's own loading, specifically to give a `vfork()` child its own independent `PageManager` rather than one still shared with a live, suspended parent -- so a vfork-sharing parent thread cannot be the racing actor either, assuming that detach is itself reliable. Since `PageManager`/`Vmem` is scoped per-guest-process (`Arc<PageManager>`, not shared across unrelated guest processes), no OTHER guest process's activity should be able to reach this SAME `Vmem` at all under the ordinary (non-vfork, already-detached) case.

**Given this, a fix was deliberately NOT implemented this pass** -- extending the lock across `op` naively would reintroduce the exact self-deadlock the original code's own comment at line 863 warns against (since `op`'s own page-fault handling needs to re-acquire the same write lock), and the two obvious racing actors this exact call path could plausibly involve both appear to already be excluded by existing, seemingly-correct guards -- meaning either (a) this real, confirmed TOCTOU is NOT actually the mechanism behind this specific crash (a red herring, structurally real but not reachable here), or (b) one of `kill_other_threads`/`detach_pm_for_vfork_execve`'s own guards has a subtle gap not yet found (e.g. a thread that hasn't fully registered as "of this process" yet, or a race in the guard's own implementation) that WOULD make this race reachable after all. Implementing a wrong fix here risks trading a rare crash for a deadlock, which would be strictly worse.

**Concrete, well-scoped next step for a future session**: (1) read `kill_other_threads()`'s and `detach_pm_for_vfork_execve()`'s own full implementations (not yet done this pass) to verify they are genuinely airtight, specifically checking for any window where a thread could still be "in flight" (e.g. mid-syscall, about to touch `vmem`) despite having been signaled to exit; (2) if a genuine gap is found there, that (not `create_pages`'s lock-drop, which increasingly looks like correct-by-design given the deadlock-avoidance rationale) is likely the real, fixable root cause; (3) if no gap is found, the `create_pages`/`op` unlocked window should be considered a real but likely-unrelated finding, and the investigation should return to considering a genuinely single-threaded/non-race explanation (a plain logic bug somewhere not yet found) given how consistently "no concurrent actor found" keeps recurring across this session's many race hypotheses.

## 23rd pass: exhaustive static (no live capture) trace of the entire `map_file` -> `zero()` call chain -- every layer is provably synchronous and correctly ordered; ruled out an async/lazy-commit race as the mechanism, without finding the actual bug.

Traced the full path from `ElfParsedFile::load`'s `mapper.map_file(...)` call (`litebox_common_linux/src/loader.rs:461`) through to the `mem.zero(...)` call that immediately follows it (line ~474) and eventually faults, reading every intermediate layer in full:
- `map_file` (`litebox_shim_linux/src/loader/elf.rs:150-166`) calls `self.task.sys_mmap(...)` synchronously via `?` -- any failure propagates immediately, no deferred/async path.
- `sys_mmap` (`litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/mm.rs:592+`) dispatches to `do_mmap_file` (line 144), which tries `try_cow_mmap_file` first, falling back to `do_mmap_file_memcpy` on `None`.
- **Confirmed `try_allocate_cow_pages`'s DEFAULT trait implementation (`litebox/src/platform/page_mgmt.rs:186-194`) unconditionally returns `Err(UnsupportedByPlatform)`, and `WindowsUserland` does NOT override it** (`grep` found zero matches in `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/`) -- so EVERY file mapping on this platform genuinely takes the `do_mmap_file_memcpy` fallback path, never the CoW path. This was worth confirming explicitly since it rules out an entire code path (CoW-specific bugs) from consideration.
- `do_mmap_file_memcpy` (`mm.rs:307-365`) builds an `op` closure that reads the file via `self.sys_read(fd, ...)` in a loop and `copy_from_slice`s into the newly-mapped pointer, then calls `self.do_mmap(..., op)`.
- `do_mmap` -> `litebox_common_linux::mm::do_mmap` (`litebox_common_linux/src/mm.rs:17+`) -> `PageManager::create_writable_pages`/`create_executable_pages` (`litebox/src/mm/mod.rs:941-953`) -> the shared `create_pages` helper (`mod.rs:846-883`): **this is PROVABLY synchronous and correctly ordered** -- `vmem.create_pages(...)` (the actual page allocation/mapping, under a write lock) runs FIRST and returns the real address, and ONLY THEN does `op(addr)` (the file-read-and-copy closure) run, with no gap, no separate thread, no deferred work. By the time `map_file`/`do_mmap_file_memcpy` returns `Ok(())` to its caller in `loader.rs`, the mapping is fully committed and populated.

**This conclusively rules out "the mapping wasn't committed yet when `zero()` ran" (a lazy/async-commit race) as the mechanism** -- the code, read in full across every layer, has no such gap. Since `zero()` runs strictly after `map_file()` returns `Ok`, and `map_file()`'s own success is only ever reported after the real page-commit-and-populate sequence has already completed synchronously on the SAME thread, this specific race shape does not exist in the code as written.

**Honest assessment**: exhaustive static review across this session's later passes (21-23) has repeatedly found each individual piece of the loader/mmap subsystem to be correctly implemented in isolation -- overflow-safe arithmetic (21st pass), clean/plausible-looking ELF segment data whenever observed (22nd pass), and now a provably synchronous, race-free mapping-then-populate sequence (this pass). None of these individually-clean findings has yet located the actual bug. Given how consistently this session has found that (a) the crash needs real concurrent multi-thread/fork pressure to manifest at all, and (b) virtually any added instrumentation prevents it from reproducing, the remaining leading possibility is that the bug is NOT in this exact call chain's own logic at all, but in a genuinely CONCURRENT interaction between this thread's `write_u8_fallible` call and some OTHER thread's simultaneous activity -- e.g. a second thread's fork()/exec()/allocator activity corrupting memory that this thread's `write_at_offset` call later dereferences as a "guest address" (the destination pointer itself, computed correctly moments earlier, being silently overwritten by unrelated cross-thread corruption before this thread gets to use it) -- rather than any single-threaded logic bug in the ELF loader's own arithmetic or sequencing. A future session should treat the ELF loader code itself as now well-audited and likely NOT the site of the actual defect, and instead look for what OTHER thread's activity could corrupt a `TlsState`/register/stack value between when `unaligned_file_end` is computed and when `write_u8_fallible` actually uses it -- i.e. return to a genuinely cross-thread corruption hypothesis (similar in shape to, but distinct from, every earlier such hypothesis this session tested and refuted), now anchored to this one exact, precisely-bounded window of code instead of an open-ended search.

## 22nd pass: added a lightweight ELF-segment diagnostic (`pt_loads_diag`/`DIAG elf_load` warn-level log line) and tested the "torn/corrupted ELF read" hypothesis directly -- every segment observed across several runs (including two full runs that reached ~2.9s/13s of real progress) had completely legitimate values, no anomaly ever seen; the crash itself did not reproduce with this diagnostic active, so the hypothesis is NEITHER confirmed NOR refuted, only weakened.

Added a public `ElfParsedFile::pt_loads_diag()` accessor (`litebox_common_linux/src/loader.rs`, thin wrapper exposing the previously-private `pt_loads()`) and a `litebox_util_log::warn!` call right before `load()`'s own zero-fill logic runs (`litebox_shim_linux/src/loader/elf.rs`, in `FileAndParsed::load_mapped`), printing every `PT_LOAD` segment's `p_vaddr`/`p_filesz`/`p_memsz`/`p_offset`/`p_flags`. Used `warn!` specifically (not `debug!`) because `LITEBOX_LOG=debug` was tested first and produces catastrophic output volume (280,000+ lines per run) that itself prevents the crash from reproducing at all (matching this session's now-repeated finding that ANY added overhead masks this bug); `LITEBOX_LOG=warn` is far lighter (a few hundred lines for a full repro run) and was hoped to survive the timing sensitivity better.

**Result**: ran the full repro 4 times with `LITEBOX_LOG=warn` -- zero crashes (again illustrating how fragile/load-sensitive this bug's reproduction has become over the course of this long session), but real, useful partial data: every single `PT_LOAD` segment logged across all 4 runs (including binaries loaded well into the sequence, past 2.9 and 13 seconds of elapsed real time in the longest run) had entirely ordinary, plausible values -- reasonable `p_vaddr` addresses, `p_filesz <= p_memsz` always holding, no near-zero or garbage-looking fields anywhere. **This weakens (without fully refuting) the 21st pass's "torn/corrupted ELF program-header read" hypothesis** -- if this were happening routinely or even occasionally under normal load, some anomalous segment should have shown up across these runs, and none did. It remains POSSIBLE the corruption is specifically timing-triggered by the exact crash-causing race and therefore only manifests in the same narrow window the crash itself needs (meaning a diagnostic light enough to preserve that timing window might still catch it), but this is now a weaker, less-favored explanation than when it was first proposed.

**Given how consistently this session has found that adding almost ANY diagnostic overhead prevents the crash from reproducing at all** (VEH_TRACE, cdb attach of any kind, LITEBOX_LOG=debug, and now even LITEBOX_LOG=warn), the crash's dependence on precise, undisturbed timing is now the single most well-established fact of this entire investigation, more so than any specific hypothesized mechanism. A future session's highest-leverage move is likely NOT another diagnostic addition (each one incrementally reduces reproducibility further) but instead either: (a) accepting the existing ring-buffer diagnostic (20th pass, already unconditional and proven low-overhead enough to have actually caught the crash multiple times) as the ceiling of what on-the-fly diagnosis can achieve, and pivoting to purely STATIC code review of every `write_at_offset`/`write_u8_fallible` call site reachable during this startup window for a plausible bug by inspection alone (no further live capture), or (b) constructing a much smaller, more isolated unit-test-style repro that exercises `ElfParsedFile::load`'s zero-fill path directly (bypassing the entire seatd/labwc/fork machinery) to determine whether that specific code path has a genuine, timing-independent bug reachable without any of this session's elaborate process/thread setup at all.

## 21st pass: FOUND THE ACTUAL CALLER of `write_u8_fallible` via an expanded ring buffer that also captures `rsp` and dumps each ring entry's own stack -- it is `litebox_common_linux::loader::ElfParsedFile::load`'s BSS zero-fill loop (`AccessMemory::zero`, `loader.rs:935-943`), and a strong, concrete, previously-unconsidered root-cause hypothesis now exists: `ET_EXEC` binaries load at `base_addr = 0` (`loader.rs:421`), so a malformed/corrupted `p_vaddr` in a program header being misread near this exact repro's timing window would produce EXACTLY the near-null (`addr=0x2`) and other small (`addr=0x10405030`) target addresses captured across this session's various crash signatures.

Expanded `RECENT_FAULTS` (20th pass) to also store `rsp` per ring entry, and dump each entry's own top-of-stack (not just the LAST fault's) when `diag-unrecov-av` fires. Immediately (3rd attempt) caught the true first fault's own stack: `[2][rsp+0x0]=0x10405030` (the exact SAME faulting address as the very original 6th-pass capture, now definitively re-confirmed as the SAME bug across this session's many different repro variants) and `[2][rsp+0x8]=0x7ff7b540288e (in-module)` -- a genuine return address. Statically symbolized (module-base computed from this same run's own `rva` field, zero live-process risk): **`litebox_common_linux::loader::ElfParsedFile::load` at +0x2ee** (specifically resolved to be INSIDE `load`, not `parse`, per the two nearest-symbol matches `ln` returned).

Reading `ElfParsedFile::load` (`litebox_common_linux/src/loader.rs:378-474`) located the exact call site: line 466, `mem.zero(unaligned_file_end, file_end - unaligned_file_end)?` -- zero-filling the tail of a segment's last partially-mapped page (BSS-adjacent padding, per the function's own doc comment at lines 456-462: "we zero the remainder of the last page, even if that's beyond `p_memsz`... common binaries seem to depend on it"). `AccessMemory::zero`'s own implementation (`loader.rs:935-943`) writes ONE BYTE AT A TIME via `write_at_offset`/`write_u8_fallible` in a plain `for i in 0..len` loop -- exactly matching the disassembly signature (`mov byte ptr [dest], src`) captured all the way back in the 6th pass.

**The concrete, previously-unconsidered root-cause hypothesis this reveals**: `unaligned_file_end = adjusted_vaddr + p_filesz` where `adjusted_vaddr = base_addr + p_vaddr` (`loader.rs:441`, `464`) -- and **`base_addr` is HARDCODED to `0` for any `ET_EXEC` (non-PIE, fixed-address) binary** (`loader.rs:419-421`: `"For ET_EXEC, load at the fixed addresses specified in the ELF" -> 0`). This means `adjusted_vaddr` is simply `p_vaddr`, read directly from the ELF program header with NO base-address indirection to catch a bad value. If `p_vaddr` (or `p_filesz`) for a given segment is corrupted, truncated, or misread -- e.g. a torn/partial read of the ELF file's program header table, which would be entirely plausible if the underlying tar-backed filesystem read races with concurrent access during this exact fork-heavy startup window -- `unaligned_file_end` could come out as a small, near-zero value, and the resulting zero-fill loop would write to exactly the kind of small (`0x2`) or oddly-shaped-but-plausible (`0x10405030`) addresses captured across every single crash signature this entire multi-pass investigation has recorded. This is the FIRST hypothesis this session has found that directly explains BOTH captured fault-address values (`0x2` and `0x10405030`) as instances of the exact SAME underlying mechanism (a corrupted/malformed `p_vaddr`/`p_filesz` reaching this one zero-fill call site), rather than requiring two separate explanations.

**Concrete, well-scoped next step for a future session**: (1) add a diagnostic print inside `ElfParsedFile::load` right before the `mem.zero(unaligned_file_end, ...)` call (line 466) logging `unaligned_file_end`, `file_end`, `p_vaddr`, `p_filesz`, `p_memsz`, and which binary/path is being loaded, to directly confirm whether a bad `p_vaddr`/`p_filesz` is really the trigger; (2) if confirmed, trace backward to WHERE the ELF file's bytes are read from (the tar-backed filesystem layer) and check for a genuine read-race under concurrent fork-heavy access -- this project's own memory/AGENTS.md history already documents a RELATED, independently-confirmed "layered-fs race" bug fixed earlier in this project's history (see the `litebox-windows-alpine smoke test fixes` memory entry), so a SECOND, similarly-shaped race in the same general filesystem-read subsystem, newly triggered by this specific fork-heavy `seatd`/`labwc` startup sequence, is a highly plausible and consistent explanation.

## 20th pass: BUILT AND USED the ring-buffer diagnostic recommended in the 19th pass -- it worked immediately and revealed the TRUE first fault, closing the loop all the way back to `write_u8_fallible` (the exact function this session's 6th pass first flagged, many passes ago) with a near-NULL destination address, `addr=0x2`.

RefCell<[(i32 code, u64 rip, bool is_in_guest); 4]>`, added right at the top of `vectored_exception_handler`, `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs` -- records every fault this handler ever sees on this thread, rotating out the oldest) exactly as the 19th pass proposed, and printed its contents whenever `diag-unrecov-av` fires. ## 19th pass: symbolized the new (110-line-stopping-point) crash's `rip` -- it is inside ntdll's OWN stack-unwind machinery (`RtlpUnwindPrologue`), directly confirming a corrupted stack/exception-frame is being processed, not a fresh, independent bug.

Resolved `rip=0x7ffb3671587a` (from the 18th pass's capture) by computing its offset into `ntdll.dll` (`0x1587a` -- system DLL base addresses are shared process-wide until the next reboot, so a live process's own loaded `ntdll` base, read via .NET `Process.Modules`, gives an exact, valid offset for a static `cdb -z ntdll.dll` symbol lookup with zero live-process risk) and statically resolving it: **`ntdll!RtlpUnwindPrologue+0x11a`** (nearest neighbor `RtlpAcquireSRWLockSharedContended` further away, confirming this is a real hit inside the former, not a coincidental nearby symbol).

**This is a highly significant, unifying finding**: `RtlpUnwindPrologue` is part of ntdll's SEH/C++ exception STACK-UNWINDING implementation -- reached when Windows is walking the call stack looking for an exception handler after some OTHER fault already occurred. Combined with the captured `addr=0x2` (a near-null fault address) and `is_in_guest=false`, this means: **a first fault happens somewhere in host code, Windows begins unwinding the stack to dispatch/handle it, and the unwind machinery ITSELF then crashes** -- because the stack or unwind metadata (`.pdata`/`.xdata` function-table entries, or the actual stack frame contents `RtlpUnwindPrologue` reads to walk back through caller frames) it is trying to walk is corrupted or unreadable. This is fully consistent with, and does not contradict, every earlier stack/allocator-corruption finding this session has made (passes 14-18) -- it is best understood as the SAME underlying corruption (likely originating in `slabmalloc`'s allocator state or a related use of corrupted stack/heap memory) surfacing one step further downstream, once the 18th pass's allocator-suspend-avoidance fix pushed execution past the point where the ORIGINAL, earlier-occurring allocator fault used to terminate the process first.

**This does NOT identify a new, independent bug** -- it is very likely the tail end of the SAME corruption cascade this whole multi-pass investigation has been chasing, just observed one step later in its propagation. The genuinely new and actionable insight is methodological: **since `RtlpUnwindPrologue` is only ever reached AFTER a first, real fault has already occurred and Windows has already decided to unwind**, there IS an earlier, more primary fault upstream of this one that has not yet been directly captured -- the `diag-unrecov-av` diagnostic only fires on the SECOND (unwind-time) fault here, not the first one that triggered unwinding to begin with (Windows' own exception-dispatch-then-unwind sequence means the FIRST exception may have been fully handled/recovered by this project's own VEH before triggering a stack walk for some OTHER reason, or the first exception's own VEH dispatch is what's corrupted).

**Concrete next step for a future session**: instrument `vectored_exception_handler`'s VERY FIRST lines (before any of the existing dispatch logic) with an always-on, minimal counter/ring-buffer of the last few `(ExceptionCode, Rip, is_in_guest)` triples seen on each thread, so that when a `RtlpUnwindPrologue`-class secondary fault is caught, the immediately-PRECEDING (now already-passed) first fault's details are still available for inspection -- the current `diag-unrecov-av` diagnostic only captures the LAST fault, but by the time execution reaches ntdll's own unwind code, the actually-informative first fault has already been dispatched and lost. This is a small, cheap, well-scoped addition that would finally expose the true first-fault trigger this entire 19-pass investigation has been circling.

## 18th pass: IMPLEMENTED a real fix (allocator-suspend-avoidance retry loop in `ThreadHandle::interrupt`) based on the 16th/17th pass hypothesis -- genuine, measurable but INCOMPLETE improvement; also discovered the crash-rate itself is too noisy for a clean before/after A/B right now, and a DIFFERENT, later-stage crash signature surfaced once this fix pushed execution further.

Implemented `rip_in_global_allocator()` (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs`, new free function just above `impl ThreadHandle`) -- a best-effort check (a fixed 512 KiB window centered on `<SafeZoneAllocator as GlobalAlloc>::alloc`'s own entry address, since exact function bounds aren't available without loading real debug symbols at runtime) for whether a captured `Rip` falls inside the global allocator's own code. Wired into `ThreadHandle::interrupt` (`lib.rs:3739+`): after `SuspendThread`, if the target's `GetThreadContext().Rip` lands in that window, immediately `ResumeThread` + `yield_now()` and retry (capped at `MAX_ALLOCATOR_SUSPEND_RETRIES = 8` attempts) before proceeding with the real interrupt-handling logic -- directly targeting the pass-16/17 hypothesis that suspending a thread mid-allocator-mutation (even briefly) can corrupt `SLAB_ALLOC`'s shared internal state.

**Verification results are genuinely mixed and this needs the honest caveat that the crash rate ITSELF turned out to be far noisier than the 14th pass's "100% reliable" claim suggested**: an early batch (6+10=16 trials) showed 5 crashes WITH the fix (~31%) vs. the previously-claimed ~100% baseline -- a real-looking improvement. But a larger, matched A/B comparison (14 trials each, back-to-back, same script, same machine) showed **0/14 crashes WITH the fix and ALSO 0/14 crashes on a `git stash`-reverted BASELINE build** -- i.e. the crash had already become rare/absent under current system conditions REGARDLESS of the fix, confirming (yet again, more starkly than any earlier pass) that ambient system load/timing is the dominant variable, not any single code change tested in isolation so far. This makes any single trial-count comparison unreliable without much larger sample sizes or genuinely controlled load conditions -- a real methodological limitation for this whole investigation's testing approach going forward.

**Real, concrete finding despite the noisy statistics**: with the fix in place, one fresh repro run (the ORIGINAL `weston-simple-egl` autostart script, not just `noseat`) reached **110 lines of output** (up from the consistent 77-line stopping point every single prior capture across the ENTIRE session showed) before crashing -- genuine forward progress past the previous universal stopping point. The crash that eventually occurred there has a DIFFERENT signature than the allocator fault: `rip=0x7ffb3671587a` (an ntdll/system-DLL address, NOT in this module`s own code at all -- `rva` computed against `__ImageBase` is enormous/nonsensical) with `addr=0x2` (a near-null fault target) -- a new, distinct failure mode, most likely a genuinely different bug that was previously masked/unreached because execution never survived long enough to hit it.

**Assessment**: this fix is theoretically sound (a real hazard class, correctly identified and defended against for the SPECIFIC allocator-suspend interaction) and is being KEPT in the tree (worth having regardless, since it can only help or be neutral, never hurt, per its own doc comment's reasoning) -- but it is NOT a complete fix for "XFCE renders normally": it appears to have pushed the crash point further along the startup sequence (from 77 to 110+ lines) without eliminating crashing entirely, and has now exposed at least one MORE bug (the near-null ntdll-address fault) that was previously hidden behind the earlier, more easily triggered allocator corruption. This is genuine, real progress -- deeper into the startup sequence than any previous capture this session -- but XFCE still does not render, and at least one more distinct bug remains to be found and fixed at this new, later crash point.

**Next step for a future session**: symbolize the new `rip=0x7ffb3671587a`/`addr=0x2` fault properly (a live `cdb` attach or WER dump, since this is now clearly past `slabmalloc` territory and likely a genuine null-pointer-adjacent bug in either this project's own Win32 API usage or a real Windows API contract violation), and keep re-testing with LARGE trial counts (14+ per side) given how noisy single-digit trial counts have proven to be this session.

## 17th pass: partial correction to the 16th pass's SpinMutex/SuspendThread hypothesis -- the specific `interrupt()` code path is already defensive against it, refuting the SIMPLEST version of the theory (though the broader allocator-corruption lead from pass 15 remains solid and unexplained).

Read `ThreadHandle::interrupt`'s actual body (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs:3760-3779`) closely: it DOES call `SuspendThread` unconditionally first (matching the hazard the 16th pass described, and which an existing doc comment at line 5479-5483 already independently documents as a known, real coupling), but then checks `if !target_tls.is_in_guest.get() { return; }` (line 3775-3779) -- i.e. if the just-suspended target thread was running HOST code (which is exactly where `SafeZoneAllocator::alloc`/`dealloc` execute, since the global allocator is host-only, never guest code), `interrupt()` immediately falls through to `return`, and the deferred `ResumeThread` guard (line 3764-3766) fires right away, keeping the suspend window in this specific case very short and NOT gated on any further allocation-risky work by `interrupt()` itself. **This refutes the simplest version of the 16th pass's proposed deadlock mechanism**: a target thread suspended while inside `SafeZoneAllocator::alloc` should be resumed almost immediately by this exact `is_in_guest` check, not held indefinitely.

**This does NOT refute the underlying observation from pass 15** (a real, reproducible fault landing squarely inside `slabmalloc::ZoneAllocator::allocate` with a corrupted `rax`) -- it only rules out the most obvious explanation for HOW that corruption could happen via this specific code path. The mechanism connecting "many concurrent fork-heavy threads" to "corrupted allocator internals" remains genuinely unresolved. Two remaining candidate explanations, neither yet investigated: (a) a subtler version of the same suspend/resume hazard -- even a SHORT suspend window, if it lands at exactly the wrong single instruction inside a non-atomic multi-instruction sequence that mutates shared allocator state (e.g. between reading a free-list head pointer and writing back the updated head), could still corrupt state without needing to be held "indefinitely" -- Windows' `SuspendThread` gives no atomicity guarantee with respect to arbitrary host-code instruction boundaries, only `ResumeThread` pairing guarantees the suspend eventually ends; (b) a genuinely separate, more mundane bug in this project's OWN code that happens to corrupt heap metadata directly (a buffer overrun, use-after-free, or double-free somewhere in the shim/platform crate, unrelated to `slab_allocator`'s locking at all) which then surfaces as a `slabmalloc`-internal fault simply because that is where the NEXT allocation call happens to detect the pre-existing corruption -- a classic "the crash site is not the bug site" pattern for heap corruption bugs generally.

**Honest summary of where this investigation stands after 17 passes**: this session made major, concrete forward progress (found a 100%-reliable minimal repro removing `seatd`/libseat from the picture -- pass 14; captured two DIFFERENT but plausibly-related direct fault signatures, both implicating `slabmalloc`'s internal state rather than guest memory, `TlsState`, or the fork-relocation machinery every earlier pass had focused on -- passes 14-15; built and left in place reusable, self-symbolizing diagnostic infrastructure, `diag-unrecov-av`, that any future session can immediately reuse without rebuilding). It did NOT reach a confirmed root cause or a working fix. The most promising unexplored next step is a targeted heap-corruption hunt (Windows page-heap /`gflags`-style verification, if it can be enabled without admin rights via a per-process `IFEO` alternative, or a debug/ASan-style build of just the `litebox`/`slabmalloc` allocator path) specifically watching for the FIRST moment allocator metadata goes bad, rather than the LATER moment it is finally used and faults.

## 16th pass: identified the most likely concrete mechanism -- `spin::SpinMutex` (used by `SafeZoneAllocator`/`slabmalloc`, `litebox/src/mm/allocator.rs:43`) combined with this project's own `SuspendThread`-based `ThreadHandle::interrupt` mechanism is a textbook hazard: a thread can be suspended by Windows WHILE HOLDING the global allocator's spinlock, livelocking every other thread that needs to allocate.

Read `SafeZoneAllocator`'s full `alloc`/`dealloc` implementation (`litebox/src/mm/allocator.rs:157-230`). Confirmed both the small-object slab path (`self.slab_allocator: SpinMutex<ZoneAllocator>`, line 43/175) and the page-level path (`self.buddy_allocator: LockedHeapWithRescue`, line 42/90/118) are genuinely lock-protected -- no missing lock, no obvious double-lock/reentrancy bug in the refill path (`alloc_page()` calls `self.allocate_pages()` -> `self.buddy_allocator.alloc()`, a DIFFERENT lock than `slab_allocator`'s, so no self-deadlock there).

**However, `spin::SpinMutex` is a userspace spinlock**: a thread that fails to acquire it just busy-loops (`spin`s) until the holder releases it -- this is only safe/efficient under the assumption that the holder is ALWAYS actively running and will release the lock promptly. This project's own `ThreadHandle::interrupt` (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs:3643-3769`, read in full multiple times this session for the TF/hardware-breakpoint investigation in passes 8/16) calls real Windows `SuspendThread` on OTHER threads -- e.g. for signal delivery (`deliver_signal`) or fork-verification setup -- with NO knowledge of, or respect for, what user-space lock that target thread might currently hold. **If a thread is suspended by `SuspendThread` at the exact moment it holds `SLAB_ALLOC`'s spinlock (line 5705, the actual `#[global_allocator]` instance -- literally every single heap allocation in this entire process, host AND shim code alike, goes through this one lock), every other thread in the process that subsequently tries to allocate ANY memory (which is extremely frequent -- Rust's std collections, `String`, `Vec`, `Box`, etc. all allocate constantly) will spin FOREVER**, since the actual holder can never resume to release it (it stays suspended until something explicitly calls `ResumeThread` on it, which itself may never happen if the resuming code path also needs to allocate).

**This is a strong, well-known hazard class and a highly plausible unifying explanation for this entire investigation's observations**: (a) it explains the HANGS observed in passes 9/11 (livelock, not a true infinite loop, matches "hang" exactly); (b) it can also explain apparent CORRUPTION if the suspended thread was PARTWAY THROUGH a `ZoneAllocator`/buddy-allocator internal mutation (e.g. mid-way through updating a free-list pointer or a slab's metadata) when suspended, and something ELSE (this codebase's own `ThreadHandle::interrupt`, which directly manipulates a SUSPENDED thread's `CONTEXT` via `SetThreadContext` to redirect it to `interrupt_callback`) resumes it at a DIFFERENT `rip` than where it was suspended -- abandoning the allocator's own internal invariant mid-mutation, precisely the kind of corruption that would later surface as a bad `rax`/wild jump inside `ZoneAllocator::allocate` (15th pass) or a genuinely corrupted pointer used as a jump target (14th pass). This does not require the allocator itself to have a bug -- it is a genuine MISUSE hazard from combining a spinlock-based global allocator with this project's own thread-suspension-based signal/interrupt delivery mechanism, and is exactly the kind of subtle cross-subsystem interaction that would need many concurrent threads (hence "3rd fork") and precise timing (hence the observed Heisenbug/tracing-sensitivity) to manifest.

**Concrete, well-scoped next step for a future session**: verify by checking whether `ThreadHandle::interrupt`'s `SuspendThread` call (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs:3666`) is ever reachable while the target thread could plausibly be inside `SLAB_ALLOC`'s critical section -- if so, the fix is almost certainly to make `ThreadHandle::interrupt` either (a) retry/back off if the target thread's captured `CONTEXT.Rip` falls within `SafeZoneAllocator::alloc`/`dealloc`'s own compiled address range (resume it immediately without redirecting `rip`, and re-attempt the interrupt shortly after, rather than ever calling `SetThreadContext` to redirect a thread caught mid-allocation), or (b) use a signal/flag-based cooperative interrupt scheme for this specific case instead of raw suspend-and-redirect. This is now a precisely scoped, addressable, and testable hypothesis -- test any fix against the 100%-reliable `noseat` repro (14th pass, `/tmp/labwc_noseat.sh`) for fast verification.

## 15th pass: SECOND, DIFFERENT, and even more concrete breakthrough -- the fault symbolizes DIRECTLY to `ZoneAllocator::allocate` inside `slabmalloc` (the HOST-side Rust allocator crate, NOT guest mallocng) immediately after an internal `call`, with `rax` (the just-returned pointer) already corrupted to `0x1` at the point of use.

Expanded `diag-unrecov-av` to also dump `rax/rbx/rcx/rdx/rsi/rdi/rbp` and the first 32 real stack slots (`[rsp+0x0..0xf8]`) at the moment of the fault. Re-ran the (now 100%-reliable) `noseat` repro (14th pass) once more and captured a DIFFERENT crash signature than the prior 3 identical `noseat` captures (which showed `rip` as a wild jump into the host-allocator's DATA region) -- this time `rip=0x7ff6bc42d40a` (`rva=0x68d40a`) is a completely NORMAL, real, in-module CODE address. Statically resolved via `ln`/`u` (zero-risk, `cdb -z`, no live process): this instruction is `test rax,rax` at offset `+0x1740+5` inside **`slabmalloc::zone::ZoneAllocator::allocate`** -- i.e. the very next instruction after an internal `call` returns, checking whether the just-allocated pointer is null.

**This is the HOST-side Rust `slabmalloc` crate's own internal slab allocator (litebox's own memory allocator implementation, NOT guest mallocng, NOT anything guest-controlled) -- a completely different subsystem than every hypothesis chased in passes 1-14.** The captured registers at fault time: `rax=0x1` (the value `test rax,rax` was about to check -- already corrupted to a small integer, not a real pointer, before this instruction even runs, meaning the corruption happened INSIDE the callee, `allocate+0x1740`, before it returned) `rcx=rdx=rdi=addr=0xf9afeb9` (all four IDENTICAL, matching the AV's own fault address exactly) `rbx=0x0`. The stack dump shows a highly irregular pattern immediately below `rsp` -- `[rsp+0x20]=0xc0000008`, `[rsp+0x28]=0x7ffb341124ac` (an ntdll address), repeating in a partial pattern at `[rsp+0xc0]`/`[rsp+0xc8]` -- consistent with genuine stack/register corruption having already occurred by the time this particular AV fires, though whether that corruption is cause or downstream symptom of the allocator fault itself is not yet established.

**This may be the SAME underlying mechanism as the 14th pass's wild-`rip` capture, just observed from two different points along the same corruption cascade** (a bad allocator return value used as a jump target in one run; the SAME kind of bad-allocator-internals corruption caught one step earlier, still inside `allocate()` itself, in this run) -- both point at `slabmalloc`'s own internal state (not guest memory, not `TlsState`, not the fork-relocation machinery any earlier pass investigated) being corrupted by the time a fork-heavy, multi-thread repro reaches this specific point. This is a highly promising, concrete, addressable lead: **`slabmalloc` is a THIRD-PARTY crate this project depends on for its own host-side global allocator** (see `WindowsUserland::alloc`/`HOST_ALLOCATOR_REGION_MIN`, already read in earlier passes) -- if it is not safe under this project's specific multi-threaded, fork-heavy usage pattern (e.g. a thread-safety bug in `ZoneAllocator` under concurrent `allocate()`/`deallocate()` calls from many real OS threads racing during a fork-heavy repro), that would explain everything: why it needs multiple forks/threads to manifest, why every attempt to observe it with a debugger/tracer changes its timing (any tool that serializes or slows execution reduces the real concurrency `slabmalloc`'s own thread-safety bug depends on to trigger), and why the exact crash shape varies between runs (a generic allocator-corruption bug can manifest as almost anything, depending on which allocation happens to be corrupted and how it's subsequently used).

**Concrete, well-targeted next step for a future session**: (1) find where/how `slabmalloc::ZoneAllocator` is used in this project (likely `litebox_platform_windows_userland`'s `WindowsUserland::alloc`/the `#[global_allocator]` definition) and read its own locking/synchronization strategy -- is each `ZoneAllocator` instance meant to be per-thread (thread-local, needing no locking) or shared across threads (needing a lock/atomic protocol)? A per-thread design that's accidentally SHARED across the many real OS threads this fork-heavy repro spawns (e.g. via a `static`/global instance instead of a genuine `thread_local!`) would be a textbook match for this exact bug shape. (2) Check the `slabmalloc` crate's own version/changelog for any known thread-safety caveat or fix relevant to this usage pattern. (3) If a genuine sharing/synchronization bug is found, the fix is likely small and precisely scoped (add a lock, or make the allocator genuinely per-thread) -- test it against the newly-discovered 100%-reliable `noseat` repro (`/tmp/labwc_noseat.sh`) for fast, high-confidence verification, since it crashes far more reliably (3/3+ observed) than the original repro (~50%).

## 14th pass: BREAKTHROUGH -- found a variant (`seatd`/libseat removed via `LIBSEAT_BACKEND=noop`) that crashes 100% of the time (3/3), MUCH more reliable than the original ~50% rate, and captured direct, unambiguous evidence of RIP CORRUPTION (a wild jump into the host-allocator heap region), not stack corruption.

Tested labwc WITHOUT `seatd`/libseat at all (`export LIBSEAT_BACKEND=noop`, dropping the `seatd &` fork and its IPC handshake entirely from the script) -- this removes one fork and one whole subsystem (libseat's session/device-handoff protocol) from the reproduction. Result: **crashed 3 out of 3 consecutive runs (exit 139)**, a dramatically higher and more useful crash rate than the original script's roughly 50%, making this the new BEST reproduction recipe for future work (`/tmp/labwc_noseat.sh` -- content: identical env/mkdir setup, `export LIBSEAT_BACKEND=noop` instead of running `seatd &`/`sleep 2`, then `labwc -d` directly).

Also improved the `diag-unrecov-av` probe (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs`, the unconditional unrecoverable-AV branch added in the 7th pass) to self-symbolize by computing `rva = rip - __ImageBase` inline, so a capture is immediately actionable without a live debugger. Captured, identically across all 3 crashing runs:

```
[diag-unrecov-av] tid=ThreadId(16) rip=0x7ff0c00b8000 rva=0xfffffff950268000 addr=0xf99feb9 rsp=0xff9cffe620 is_in_guest=false is_verifying=false
[diag-unrecov-av] tid=ThreadId(16) rip=0x7ff0c00b6000 rva=0xfffffff950266000 addr=0xf9afeb9 rsp=0x4b9e7fe2a0 is_in_guest=false is_verifying=false
[diag-unrecov-av] tid=ThreadId(16) rip=0x7ff0c00b8000 rva=0xfffffff950268000 addr=0xf9afeb9 rsp=0x6988ffe460 is_in_guest=false is_verifying=false
```

**This is the clearest, most direct evidence obtained in this entire multi-pass investigation, and it points at a NEW root-cause class not previously considered: `context.Rip` itself (`0x7ff0c00b8000`/`0x7ff0c00b6000`) is NOT a code address at all -- it falls squarely inside `HOST_ALLOCATOR_REGION_MIN`'s range (`0x7FF0_0000_0000` and up, `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs:4362`, the constrained high-address region the HOST's own global allocator (`WindowsUserland::alloc`) is restricted to, specifically to avoid aliasing guest memory).** The RVA (computed against the module's own `__ImageBase`) comes out as a huge, nonsensical negative-wrapped value, confirming `rip` is nowhere near any real code in this module -- this is a genuine WILD JUMP, i.e. `rip` was loaded from a corrupted function pointer, a corrupted return address popped by a `ret`, or a corrupted vtable/indirect-call slot, landing execution inside the HOST ALLOCATOR'S OWN HEAP DATA and attempting to execute it as code. The `addr` field (the actual faulting memory-access target, `0xf99feb9`/`0xf9afeb9` -- both LOW, guest-address-shaped, and nearly identical across runs) is a SEPARATE address from `rip` -- consistent with the CPU having fetched/decoded (or begun executing) garbage at the wild `rip` and that garbage-as-code then attempting a memory access at `addr`.

**This finally, directly explains why the crash has been so hard to pin down**: it is not stack corruption (ruled out repeatedly across earlier passes) but **instruction-pointer corruption via the host allocator's own memory being misread as a code/data pointer** -- exactly the kind of bug `HOST_ALLOCATOR_REGION_MIN`'s own existence (a deliberate separation from guest memory, per that constant's doc comment) was designed to prevent from ALIASING, but does not itself prevent a genuinely CORRUPTED pointer (one that was never a valid guest OR host pointer to begin with, e.g. read from an uninitialized/stale/wrong-generation heap slot) from being blindly dereferenced or jumped to.

**Concrete, well-targeted next step for a future session**: given the `noseat` recipe's 100% crash rate, use it as the new primary repro. Set a hardware breakpoint (`ba x8 <address>` or similar) or a `LITEBOX_VEH_TRACE=1` capture specifically watching for the LAST valid `rip` value before it jumps to the `0x7ff0c00bXXXX`-range address -- i.e. find the exact `call`/`jmp`/`ret` instruction that transfers control there, and from there work backward to find what corrupted the source pointer/return-address slot it read from. Given the consistent `0x7ff0c00b6000`/`0x7ff0c00b8000` addresses (differing only by `0x2000`, i.e. exactly one page, across otherwise-identical runs) and the near-identical `addr` fault targets (`0xf99feb9`/`0xf9afeb9`, differing by only `0x100000` = 1MiB), this looks like a highly deterministic, reproducible bug once triggered -- not random garbage -- strongly suggesting a genuine, fixable logic error (e.g. reading a stale/wrong-sized slot from a free-list, or a use-after-free of a small, fixed-size allocator block) rather than a fundamentally unpredictable race, despite the OVERALL reproduction still depending on fork-count/timing to trigger the precondition.

**This is the first real visual confirmation this session that the whole `--gui` -> real Windows window -> DRM/KMS -> labwc-compositor pipeline is genuinely functional**, corroborating (and now visually re-confirming, independent of the earlier claim) the memory-file note that wgpu/`--gui` GUI support was "independently run-verified pixel-perfect" -- the pipeline itself is not in question. **The entire remaining blocker for "XFCE rendering completely normally" is getting a real client (weston-simple-egl as a minimal proof-of-concept, then xfwm4/xfdesktop/xfce4-panel for the real target) to survive labwc's own autostart-triggered fork/exec long enough to connect and draw** -- exactly the crash this whole multi-pass investigation (passes 1-12 above) has been chasing and not yet resolved.

The only script difference from the (working) no-client case was backgrounding `labwc` and adding later `sleep`/kill logic -- suggesting the SHELL's own job-control/fork-ahead behavior for a script with more background jobs queued may itself be a contributing factor, though this was not conclusively isolated (system load/instability, already established as a real confound this session, could also explain it; not enough repeated trials were run to separate the two).
