## 12th pass: correction to the 11th pass's "sys_write calls PageManager::duplicate" finding -- likely a `~*k` stack-walker artifact, not a real call relationship. `PageManager::duplicate`'s own safety contract rules out it ever legitimately being called from an ordinary syscall.

Statically verified via `ln` (list-nearest-symbol, zero-risk, no live process needed) that the captured return address genuinely falls within `sys_write`'s real compiled byte range (confirmed against the next real symbol, `do_flock`, which is far away) -- so it is not a wrong-module/wrong-symbol lookup. However, reading `litebox/src/mm/mod.rs:776`'s `PageManager::duplicate` directly shows its own doc comment is unambiguous: `# Safety: The caller must ensure no other code is concurrently mutating memory tracked by self for the duration of this call (e.g. other threads of the same process must be stopped)` -- this is EXCLUSIVELY a `fork()`-time operation by design, structurally incompatible with being reachable from an ordinary, concurrently-issued `write()` syscall (which by definition runs while other threads keep running normally).

The much more likely explanation: cdb's `~*k` uses a HEURISTIC stack walker when precise unwind metadata is unavailable or the frame-pointer chain is ambiguous (common in heavily-optimized/inlined release Rust code) -- it can misattribute a stale, already-returned call's leftover return address on the stack as a "real" frame, especially in a large, many-closures function like `do_write` (spans `litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/file.rs:1316-2185`, ~900 lines, almost certainly deeply inlined across `run_on_raw_fd`'s per-fd-type closures). The apparent "sys_write -> PageManager::duplicate" call is most likely exactly this kind of stack-walker misattribution -- a leftover, stale return address from an EARLIER call (elsewhere on the same thread's real call history, e.g. this same thread's own prior `fork()`/`clone()` handling) sitting in memory near `sys_write`'s own frame, not a genuine live call chain.

**This does not fully retract the 11th pass's underlying observation** (a thread was captured mid-syscall inside `allocate_pages`/`VirtualQuery`, which IS real activity, not fabricated) -- only its `sys_write`-attribution should be treated with caution. A future session wanting to pursue this should use `cdb`'s `.frame`/`dv`/`k =` with an explicit, precise frame pointer, or a debug (not release) build's more reliable unwind info, rather than trusting `~*k`'s default heuristic walk at face value for large/heavily-inlined functions -- this is a general methodological note for ALL of this session's stack captures, not just this one, and worth remembering for any future `cdb`-based investigation of this codebase.

## 11th pass: system load from many consecutive repro attempts was itself converting the fast crash into a much-more-reproducible HANG at the identical stopping point -- caught a live snapshot mid-hang via non-invasive `cdb -pv` attach (zero perturbation risk, since it doesn't suspend/control the process), revealing a genuinely unusual `sys_write` -> `Vmem::duplicate` call path worth flagging precisely for a future session.

After many consecutive repro runs in this session, the SAME 77-line/last-line-"run session script /etc/xdg/labwc/autostart" stopping point started manifesting as a 100%-reproducible HANG (`timeout` killing it after 20s) instead of the historical ~50% fast-crash (exit 139) -- 18+ consecutive non-crashing runs in a row, a real, measured behavior shift (not chance) most likely caused by cumulative system load/resource pressure from this session's own extensive repeated testing (disk was observed at 99% full, 33GB free of 1.9TB, though free RAM was reasonable at ~8GB/16GB). This is consistent with -- and further confirms -- the whole bug being a genuine timing-sensitive race whose outcome (fast crash vs. hang vs., presumably under lighter load, success) depends on exactly how the race resolves under ambient system timing.

Used this opportunity productively: attached `cdb -pv -p <pid>` (non-invasive mode -- examines the process without suspending it or taking control, unlike a normal attach, so it cannot itself perturb the hang) to an ALREADY-HUNG process and dumped every thread's stack (`~*k`). Found:
- The outer `/bin/sh` thread (running `run_thread_inner`, i.e. the FIRST/bootstrap-process code path, not `thread_start`) blocked in `sys_wait4` -- exactly expected, since `labwc -d` runs in the script's foreground and the shell is waiting for it.
- A `pty_ioctl` thread blocked in `FutexManager::wait` -> `RawMutex::block` -> `WaitOnAddress` -- plausible for a foreground TTY compositor with no real controlling terminal signaling it, likely benign/expected for this specific `--gui`-less-console repro shape.
- **The most interesting find**: a thread stopped mid-syscall inside `sys_write` -> `litebox::mm::PageManager::duplicate` -> `Vmem::duplicate` -> `insert_mapping` -> `allocate_pages` -> `VirtualQuery` (`litebox_shim_linux::syscalls::file::sys_write`'s frame is directly visible in the captured stack, `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs`'s `allocate_pages`/`do_query_on_region` below it). A plain `write()` syscall calling into `Vmem`/`PageManager::duplicate()` -- machinery whose name and every other call site so far in this investigation is `fork()`-specific -- is structurally unexpected and had not been noticed before this capture. **This may be entirely legitimate** (e.g. a copy-on-write fault-handling path shared between `fork()` and an ordinary write into a COW-mapped page, which would be a completely normal, correct design) or it may be a genuine bug (a write syscall accidentally triggering full fork-style address-space duplication logic it has no business calling). This was NOT further investigated due to session time constraints -- a second snapshot attempt 3 seconds later found the process had exited entirely (this specific thread ID no longer existed), so whether it was genuinely stuck there or just transiently executing that path when sampled was not resolved.

**Concrete next step for a future session**: read `sys_write`'s full implementation (`litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/file.rs`, the frame offset in the captured stack was `+0x3325` into `sys_write`, a very large offset suggesting a substantial function or heavy inlining) to determine PRECISELY under what condition a plain write() call invokes `PageManager::duplicate()` -- is this a real, correct, existing, intentional code path (e.g. genuine COW-page-fault handling triggered by a `write()` into a page shared since a prior `fork()`), or is it a mistaken/accidental call that only makes sense for `fork()` proper? If the former, this specific path deserves its own live capture (watch specifically for this call, since it uniquely combines "ordinary syscall someone is likely calling very frequently" with "expensive full-address-space-duplication-adjacent logic" -- a strong candidate for BOTH a performance problem and, if any correctness issue exists in the COW machinery, this specific fork-adjacent crash). Given system load itself changed this bug's manifestation (crash -> hang) over the course of one session, a future session should also actively CONTROL for ambient system load (e.g. explicitly check free disk/RAM before each repro attempt, run repro attempts from a clean/cooled-down state rather than back-to-back) since it has now been directly observed to change the bug's presentation.

## 10th pass: the "just bump the stack size" cheap experiment was tried and REFUTED -- 128 MiB (4x the current 32 MiB) still crashes 8/10 runs, statistically indistinguishable from the un-bumped baseline. Ruled out plain stack exhaustion as the mechanism; reverted, no source changes remain from this experiment.

Bumped both `GUEST_THREAD_STACK_SIZE` (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs`, both call sites) and `INITIAL_GUEST_THREAD_STACK_SIZE` (`litebox_runner_linux_on_windows_userland/src/lib.rs`) from 32 MiB to 128 MiB, rebuilt, and ran the plain (untraced) repro 10 times: **8 crashes, 2 successes (exit 127)** -- essentially the same failure rate as the known baseline. If simple stack exhaustion were the mechanism, a 4x reservation increase should have measurably reduced (likely eliminated) the crash rate; it did not. Reverted the change (`git checkout --`) after confirming the diagnostic instrumentation from prior passes (`diag-unrecov-av`, `diag-tls-addr`, already committed at `ced24225`) was unaffected by the revert.

**This further narrows the mechanism**: it is NOT a thread reaching the end of an undersized stack reservation through ordinary deep recursion/call-chain growth (that class of bug responds linearly to reservation size, as the EARLIER, successfully-fixed `dbus-launch` 8MiB->32MiB bug, commit `e615b0c1`, did). Combined with the 9th pass's finding (WER produces no dump at all -- the crash bypasses even the OS's own top-level crash-reporting, not just this project's VEH), the likely remaining mechanism is either: (a) a genuinely instantaneous, single-instruction catastrophic stack CORRUPTION (a single bad write to `rsp` itself, or a wild jump into unmapped code, rather than gradual exhaustion) that no reservation size can protect against, or (b) something entirely outside the guest-thread-stack model altogether -- e.g. a race in the shared, PROCESS-WIDE (not per-thread) state this session's earlier passes have already touched on (`ACTIVE_THREADS`, `CLAIMED_RANGES`, the TLS-slot-index mechanism) that manifests as an apparent stack fault but is actually a use-after-free or double-registration bug in shared bookkeeping.

**State of the investigation at the end of this session**: a very large amount of ground has been covered and multiple plausible-sounding hypotheses have been rigorously tested and REFUTED with hard, reproducible evidence (heap/stack `TlsState` aliasing; cross-thread `TlsState` sharing; TF/hardware-breakpoint leak past `fork_verify::end()`; plain stack exhaustion). The crash remains unfixed. Every static/dynamic observation method tried so far (source reading across `fork_verify.rs`/`process.rs`/`lib.rs`; `LITEBOX_VEH_TRACE=1`; live `cdb` attach, both interactive and passive-filter; WER local dumps) has either failed to capture the primary fast-path crash's actual moment of death, or has itself perturbed the race enough to prevent reproduction. **This is the central obstacle a future session must solve first**: find an observation method with low enough overhead to not disturb this specific timing-sensitive race, or find a way to make the race less timing-sensitive (e.g. deliberately reproducing it under artificial CPU/scheduling pressure to WIDEN the window rather than narrow it) so that heavier tooling becomes viable again.

## 9th pass: configured WER local crash dumps (per-user HKCU, no admin needed) -- the crash produces ZERO dump, meaning it bypasses even Windows' own top-level crash-reporting machinery, not just this project's VEH. Strong new evidence pointing at a genuine stack-overflow-class death, not an ordinary dispatched exception.

Attempted a live, low-overhead `cdb -o` attach with only a passive `sxe` auto-continue filter (no per-instruction stepping, unlike `LITEBOX_VEH_TRACE`) intended to `.dump /ma` on the fatal exception with minimal timing interference. Even this lighter-weight attach was enough to change timing and prevent the crash from reproducing across 2 full attempts (both timed out at 30-35s instead of crashing) -- confirming ANY attached debugger, however passive, perturbs this specific race. This is a genuine Heisenbug with respect to every observation method tried so far in this project (VEH_TRACE, `cdb -p` live-attach, now `cdb -o` passive-filter attach).

Pivoted to a debugger-free approach: configured Windows Error Reporting local crash dumps via the per-user registry path (`HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps\litebox_runner_linux_on_windows_userland.exe`, `DumpFolder`, `DumpType=2` full dump, `DumpCount=5` -- no admin rights needed, unlike the `HKLM` equivalent which failed with `UnauthorizedAccessException`), specifically so a genuinely UNDISTURBED, zero-runtime-overhead crash could be captured automatically by the OS itself, entirely after the fact. Ran the plain (untraced, unattached) repro until it crashed (exit 139, 77 lines, the exact long-established signature) -- **`.wfgy/crash-dumps/` remained completely empty. WER never wrote a dump at all.**

**This is a highly significant new finding**: WER's `LocalDumps` mechanism activates whenever Windows' own unhandled-exception/crash-reporting pipeline processes a process death -- covering ordinary SEH-dispatched exceptions (`EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION`, etc.) as well as most `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW` cases. Its total absence here, combined with (a) the crash never reaching `vectored_exception_handler` (7th/8th pass), (b) `STATUS_BAD_STACK` (`0xC0000028`) appearing in the one detailed capture obtained (6th pass, under `LITEBOX_VEH_TRACE`, now understood to possibly be a rarer variant given the timing sensitivity), and (c) the process dying so abruptly no crash-reporting infrastructure -- not this project's own VEH, not Windows' own WER -- ever engages, together point strongly toward a **genuine, catastrophic real-stack exhaustion or corruption event** that Windows' own OS-level crash machinery cannot cleanly report on either (a scenario where the guard page mechanism itself, or the exception-dispatch machinery's OWN stack needs, cannot be satisfied because the thread's real stack is too far gone by the time ANY handler -- host VEH or OS WER -- would need to run).

**Recommended next steps for a future session, updated given this finding**: (1) the earlier idea of a live `cdb` attach or a software trace is now confirmed unproductive -- every attach method tried perturbs timing enough to avoid the race; stop trying passive/lightweight debugger attaches, they are not lightweight enough. (2) Instead, focus on STATIC prevention: since `GUEST_THREAD_STACK_SIZE`/`INITIAL_GUEST_THREAD_STACK_SIZE` were already bumped once this project (8 MiB -> 32 MiB, commit `e615b0c1`) for an unrelated but same-SHAPED stack-overflow bug (`dbus-launch`), consider whether the SPECIFIC thread that crashes here (`ThreadId(17)`/`ThreadId(18)`-class, forked from `/bin/sh -c` running labwc's `autostart` script, itself forking `seatd`/`weston-simple-egl`) is deep enough in NESTED fork/exec history that even 32 MiB is insufficient, OR whether `fork_verify`'s own single-step healing machinery (confirmed, per the 6th/7th pass captures, to be running heavily on exactly this thread right before the crash) consumes disproportionate REAL host stack per guest instruction single-stepped, in a way that could exhaust even a large reservation on a sufficiently deep/long verification run. A blunt, cheap experiment worth trying first: bump `GUEST_THREAD_STACK_SIZE` further (e.g. to 128 MiB, matching the existing `--gui` presenter thread's own precedent) and re-run the repro 10+ times -- if the crash rate drops to zero or near-zero, that is strong (if inelegant) confirmation of the stack-exhaustion hypothesis and a real, shippable interim fix, even without ever pinning down the exact instruction that overflows.

## 8th pass: TF/hardware-breakpoint disarm hypothesis REFUTED by a dedicated subagent; `rsp`-itself-stale hypothesis checked and also does not show an obvious gap. Root cause remains open; this is the most precisely characterized state of the investigation to date.

No leftover hardware trap exists. **This hypothesis is fully refuted**, no fix applied, no source changes from this angle.

Followed the subagent's own suggested next lead (a stale/untranslated `rsp` itself, not just `rip`-adjacent slots) by re-reading `on_single_step`'s case-1 healing (fork_verify.rs:990-1043, heals `rdi` and a `ret_addr_slot` VALUE, never `rsp` the register itself) and `translate_stale_source_rip` (fork_verify.rs:492-529, heals `[rsp-8]`/`[rsp]` slot VALUES and other GPRs matching a stale `rip`, again never validates `rsp` itself against `is_in_source`). This confirmed the reactive (single-step-time) healing path genuinely has no direct `rsp`-register check -- but `rsp` is ALSO healed proactively at `fork()` time: `litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/process.rs:2527`'s `fixup_stale_stack_pointers::<Platform>(&relocations, child_ctx.rsp, ...)` call is preceded by a comment ("register translation above covers every GPR at the instant `fork()` returns") confirming `rsp` (as a GPR) is already translated before this proactive stack-slot scan even runs -- so `rsp` itself does not appear to be a currently-unaddressed gap either, at least not at the initial fork-return point. Whether `rsp` could still go stale LATER, mid-single-step-verification-window (as opposed to at the initial fork-return moment this proactive fixup covers), was not conclusively ruled in or out.

**Current, honest state of the investigation**: the fast-path (untraced) crash is completely silent -- confirmed (7th pass) it never reaches `vectored_exception_handler` at all, not even the unconditional `diag-unrecov-av` probe added specifically to survive the untraced path. The ONE detailed capture obtained (6th pass, `write_u8_fallible`/`addr=0x10405030`) only happened under `LITEBOX_VEH_TRACE=1`'s heavy tracing overhead, which has since been shown (12 consecutive untraced-vs-traced comparison runs) to itself change the crash's timing enough to make it far less likely to reproduce while tracing -- meaning that specific captured fault may be a DIFFERENT, rarer variant than the primary untraced crash, not proof of the primary mechanism. Two full hypotheses (heap/stack `TlsState` aliasing across many watchpoint passes; TF/hardware-breakpoint leak) have now been investigated in real depth and REFUTED with hard evidence. The crash's true mechanism, for the PRIMARY (untraced, reliably-reproducing) case, remains unidentified.

**Recommended next steps for a future session**, in priority order: (1) since VEH itself is never reached, investigate whether the crash happens at a point where VEH is genuinely uninstalled for this thread (a race in `AddVectoredExceptionHandler` registration timing vs. this specific forked-child thread's own lifecycle -- check `ensure_veh_installed`/wherever VEH registration happens relative to `thread_start`/`ThreadHandle::run_with_handle`'s `install_tls` call) rather than assuming VEH is always active and the fault type is simply not `EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION`; (2) attach a live debugger (`cdb -p <pid>` on a freshly-attached, ALREADY-RUNNING process, timed to the known ~10-60ms crash window, per this session's own established live-attach technique) directly to the untraced, fast-path repro -- since software tracing changes timing, only a LOW-OVERHEAD live attach (not full VEH_TRACE) has any real chance of catching the primary crash mechanism in its natural timing; (3) if a live attach also proves too invasive/timing-sensitive, consider a purely passive, zero-runtime-cost forensic approach instead -- e.g. enabling Windows Error Reporting local dumps (`HKLM\...\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps`) for this exe so a FULL POST-MORTEM crash dump is captured automatically on the next natural (untraced, undisturbed) crash, then analyze that dump offline with `cdb -z` (no live timing interference at all, since the dump is already frozen by the time analysis starts).

If a hardware breakpoint or the CPU trap flag survives past `end()`, a later single-step/hardware-breakpoint trap could fire in a context Windows' own `RtlDispatchException` machinery cannot cleanly handle (especially if it fires very early, before a normal exception frame can even be constructed) -- which would exactly explain a totally VEH-invisible, silent crash, distinct from the ordinary `EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION` class this file's existing repair machinery targets.

Dispatched a focused, read-only-first subagent to: confirm exactly what `arm_codewatch`/`arm_watchaddr_data` modify, confirm whether `end()` symmetrically undoes it, and -- if a clear, minimal, correct disarm-on-end fix is warranted -- implement AND live-verify it (5+ consecutive non-crashing repro runs, since the crash reliably reproduces roughly every 1-2 attempts on the plain/untraced path). ## 6th pass: found the REAL crash entry point (`thread_start`'s own `TlsState::new()`, not `run_thread_inner`'s), and captured a complete, precise fault trace via `LITEBOX_VEH_TRACE=1` -- root cause is now narrowed to a specific write_u8_fallible fault, subagent dispatched to pinpoint the exact call site.

**Correction to the 5th-pass entry above**: `run_thread_inner`'s `TlsState::new()` (line ~1940) is NOT the production path for thread-based fork() children or `clone()`-spawned threads at all -- that is only used for the very first/bootstrap process thread. The REAL path (confirmed by reading `ThreadProvider::spawn_thread`, `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs` ~line 2769-2826) constructs `TlsState::new()` on the SPAWNING thread (~line 2814, deliberately, per its own doc comment: any fault during construction must not run on the brand-new thread before `install_tls`), moves it by value into a `std::thread::Builder::spawn` closure, and `thread_start` (~line 2719-2762) is the real per-thread entry -- this is what both `clone()` new threads AND thread-based `fork()` children (`ThreadInitState::ForkedChild`) actually go through. Added the same `LITEBOX_DIAG_TLS_ADDR` print here too (now fires for every real thread, confirmed: this session's crashing repro consistently reaches `ThreadId(17)`/`ThreadId(18)` right at the `/etc/xdg/labwc/autostart` script's own forks, matching the long-established "needs the 3rd fork" shape).

**Real breakthrough**: with `LITEBOX_VEH_TRACE=1` (the project's own existing, pre-built full-detail exception trace, much slower than a plain run but finally captured a COMPLETE trace through an actual crash), got a precise sequence for `ThreadId(18)`:
1. `[fork_verify] tid=ThreadId(18) end` -- fork-child single-step healing completes cleanly, no errors.
2. Immediately after: a FATAL (uncaught) access violation -- `code=0xc0000005 rip=0x7ff605e997e6 addr=0x10405030 is_in_guest=false is_verifying=false`.
3. `[diag_bigfault] rip bytes: [88, 11, 31, c0, 59, c3, ...]` -- disassembles to `mov [rcx], dl` then `ret`, matching `litebox/src/mm/exception_table.rs`'s `write_u8_fallible` (`write_fn!(write_u8_fallible, u8, "mov byte ptr [{dest}], {src:l}")`) almost exactly -- a primitive SPECIFICALLY DESIGNED to survive a fault here via an exception-table entry, yet the fault escalated to fatal instead of being caught.
4. `code=0xc0000028` (`STATUS_BAD_STACK`) follows immediately, then final process death -- matching the long-established "exit 139, ~86-87 lines, zero guest fatal-signal line" signature exactly.

The `is_in_guest=false is_verifying=false` combination is the key clue: this fault happens OUTSIDE the window `vectored_exception_handler`'s most complete repair machinery expects, writing to a low, guest-address-shaped target (`0x10405030`) that is invalid at that exact moment for that exact thread. Dispatched a focused subagent (read-only tracing, no fix yet) to pin down the EXACT call site issuing this write (leading candidates: the `fork_verify::end()` tail, `run_thread_arch`'s post-fork resume prologue, or the TCB `%fs:0`/`prev`/`next` self-pointer fixup logic in `litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/process.rs` ~line 2660-2820) and why `vectored_exception_handler`'s `is_in_guest=false` fault-recovery path fails to catch it here specifically. This is the most precise, actionable lead this entire investigation (spanning many prior passes) has produced -- report to follow once the subagent returns.

## 5th pass: added a real per-thread/per-process TlsState-address diagnostic (`LITEBOX_DIAG_TLS_ADDR`) at `run_thread_inner`'s entry -- conclusively rules out the ENTIRE `TlsState`/stack-proximity investigation line, crash happens strictly EARLIER than any of it.

Added a gated `eprintln!("[diag-tls-addr] pid={} tid={:?} tls_state={:p}", ...)` (with explicit `stderr().flush()`) directly after `TlsState::new()` in `run_thread_inner` (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs`, ~line 1945), to directly observe every thread's own `&tls_state` address and PID across a real repro run, instead of continuing to infer things indirectly through cdb captures.

**Important process note for future sessions**: the first attempt at this diagnostic appeared to never fire at all, which briefly looked like ANOTHER dead end -- root cause was purely a workflow mistake in this session (a `git stash`/`stash pop` around an unrelated experiment left the OLD binary on disk for one run, and separately, all manual repro invocations must set `MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL="*"` or MSYS2's bash mangles `/bin/sh` into a Windows path and the guest program load fails with a generic `ENOENT` at `load_program` that superficially resembles a crash but is unrelated -- always rebuild AND set that env var explicitly per invocation, never assume either from a prior turn).

**Real result, once correctly built and invoked**: across two full repro runs (both ending in the expected exit 139 / silent SIGSEGV signature), the diagnostic printed **exactly once per run** -- only the very first/outer `/bin/sh` process's own thread ever reaches `run_thread_inner`. No second PID or thread -- not labwc's own internal threads, not any `weston-simple-egl`/forked-child process spawned by the autostart script -- EVER reaches this print point before the crash occurs.

**This conclusively rules out the entire watchpoint/TlsState/`guest_context_top`-proximity investigation line from the four entries above**: whatever is crashing, it happens in a forked child PROCESS strictly BEFORE that child's own `run_thread`/`run_thread_with_fork_verification` call -- i.e. before any of `TlsState`, `syscall_callback`, or `guest_context_top` are even initialized for that child. This is consistent with (and now directly corroborates) this session's much earlier, independently-established finding that the fault symbolizes to `write_u8_fallible` -- a very early, low-level fault-tolerant memory-write primitive -- and with `fork_verify.rs`'s own documented purpose (healing stale pointers in the CHILD process's freshly `WriteProcessMemory`-copied address space, which necessarily happens before the child's Rust-level `run_thread` entry point runs at all).

**Corrected next step**: stop investigating anything inside `run_thread_inner`/`syscall_callback`/`TlsState` -- none of it is reachable by the crashing child before the fault. Focus entirely on the child process's OWN startup path prior to `run_thread`: how `sys_execve`'s fork/exec machinery actually launches the new child process on Windows (likely `CreateProcess` plus `WriteProcessMemory`-based address-space duplication, per `fork_verify.rs`'s own doc comments), and instrument or breakpoint at the EARLIEST possible point in the child's own execution (process entry point / DllMain / very first few instructions of its own `main`), rather than at `run_thread_inner`, to find where between child-process creation and (never-reached) `run_thread_inner` entry the crash actually occurs.

## DEFINITIVE (4th pass) correction: this entire watchpoint lead is a dead end -- the "cross-thread aliasing" theory above is REFUTED. It is the SAME thread hitting its own routine self-write, every single time.

Added `@$tid` capture at both the breakpoint-arm point (where the watched `TlsState` address is resolved) and the watch-hit point (where the write occurs), in the same run. Result: **`arming_tid=15380` == `WATCH_HIT tid=15380`.** The thread that set up the watchpoint (by being the first to call `get_tls_ptr()` after cdb attached) is the EXACT SAME thread that later trips it, via its own completely ordinary `syscall_callback` execution writing its own `GUEST_XMM0_5` field. There are no other threads involved in this capture at all.

**This retroactively invalidates all three prior interpretations in the entries above** (heap/stack overlap, benign-but-still-suspicious write, cross-thread `TlsState` aliasing) -- none of them involved any anomaly. The watchpoint has, across four independent capture attempts (BREAKTHROUGH / CORRECTION / SECOND CORRECTION / THIRD finding), only ever demonstrated one thing: a thread runs `syscall_callback`, which writes into its own `TlsState`'s `GUEST_XMM0_5` field as designed. This is 100% expected behavior and has NOTHING to do with the fork-count crash. The technique itself (get_tls_ptr+0x40 RDX capture -> `ba w8` hardware watchpoint, now with tid capture at both ends) is validated and reusable, but this specific target (`TlsState.host_sp`'s address) was the wrong thing to watch: the crash's own thread is never guaranteed to be the one whose `get_tls_ptr` call happens to be caught first by the arming breakpoint (there is no correlation forcing the watched thread to be the one that later corrupts anything), so this approach structurally cannot observe a genuine CROSS-thread corruption even if one exists -- it only ever watches whichever single thread the breakpoint incidentally armed on.

**Real next step, now correctly scoped**: to catch actual cross-thread corruption (if that is even the right hypothesis -- it has never been confirmed, only guessed), the watchpoint must be armed on the `TlsState` address belonging to a thread OTHER than whichever one is running when the breakpoint fires -- e.g. explicitly target the Nth forked child's thread (identifiable via `ThreadHandle`/`ACTIVE_THREADS` enumeration or a `LITEBOX_DIAG`-style print of each thread's own `&tls_state` address at `run_thread_inner` entry, correlated with its OS thread id), then set the hardware watchpoint from a DIFFERENT cdb thread context or via `~<tid>` targeting, and watch for a write whose `@$tid` at hit time does NOT match the thread that owns that `TlsState`. Absent that cross-thread confirmation, there is currently NO verified evidence beyond speculation that `TlsState` corruption/aliasing is the fork-count crash's actual mechanism at all -- this avenue should be treated as unconfirmed and de-prioritized in favor of re-examining the original `write_u8_fallible` fault site and `fork_verify`'s own per-thread state directly, or a fresh, narrower repro (e.g. instrumenting `TlsState`'s own address via a debug print at `run_thread_inner` entry for every thread, correlated against the crash's exact failure point) rather than continuing to iterate on this specific watchpoint approach.

## THIRD (and precise, address-verified) finding: two DIFFERENT threads resolve to the SAME `TlsState` address -- genuine cross-thread TlsState aliasing, reproduced twice with identical `delta=1544`.

Built a corrected watchpoint script that additionally captures `rip` and disassembles the exact faulting instruction (`u rip L1`), instead of inferring intent from a static disassembly of the whole function as the two entries above did. Ran it twice (fresh repro each time): both runs independently produced **`delta=1544`** between `rsp` and the watched `TlsState` address at the moment of the hit, and both resolved the faulting instruction to:

```
litebox_runner_linux_on_windows_userland!syscall_callback+0x34:
movups xmmword ptr [r11+10h], xmm1
```

This is `syscall_callback`'s `GUEST_XMM0_5` save (source line ~2300: `movups XMMWORD PTR [r11 + {GUEST_XMM0_5} + 1*16], xmm1`), a **deliberate, legitimate write to a real `TlsState` field** (`GUEST_XMM0_5` -- see struct doc comment ~line 1968-1979) -- not a stray stack push, and not `*ctx` being filled in (both earlier entries' theories are now superseded/refuted by this precise capture). `r11` at this instruction is loaded moments earlier via `mov r11, QWORD PTR gs:[r11d*8 + TEB_TLS_SLOTS_OFFSET]` (line 2274) -- i.e. **`r11` is THIS thread's own per-thread TLS-slot value**, read fresh from its own TEB.

**The actual bug, now precisely isolated**: the watchpoint was armed on a `TlsState` address (`$t3`) resolved from ONE thread's call to `get_tls_ptr()` (the breakpoint-setting thread). The hit fired because a DIFFERENT thread's `syscall_callback` invocation computed `r11 + 0x10` to that EXACT SAME watched address. Since `r11` comes from that second thread's OWN `TlsGetValue`/TEB-slot read, **two different real OS threads' TLS slots are resolving to the identical `TlsState` pointer value** -- this is the genuine root cause: not a stack-vs-heap overlap, not a benign self-write, but literal **cross-thread `TlsState` aliasing** (two threads sharing what should be exclusively-owned, thread-local state). This exactly explains the crash's dependence on thread/fork count: with only 1-2 threads the TLS slot allocation or the underlying `TlsState` storage happens to stay distinct; by the 3rd, some path causes two threads to end up pointing at the same `TlsState` instance -- after which their `host_sp`/`host_bp`/`GUEST_XMM0_5`/etc. fields are silently shared and clobbered by whichever thread last wrote, producing exactly the observed effect (a subsequent `mov rsp, [r11+HOST_SP]` restoring a stack pointer some OTHER thread saved, corrupting execution).

**Concrete next step**: since `TlsState` itself is proven stack-local (not heap-allocated, confirmed in the entry above) and unique per `run_thread_inner` call, the aliasing must be happening at the **TLS-slot-index or TEB-slot level**, not at `TlsState`'s own storage. Prime suspects: (1) `TLS_INDEX` (`static TLS_INDEX: AtomicU32`, line 1962) being read/written non-atomically or reused incorrectly across a fork()'s child-thread setup (`ensure_tls_index()` -- check whether a forked child process re-initializes vs. inherits a stale index that then collides with a value the parent process's OS allocated for something else); (2) `install_tls`/`TlsSetValue` (line 2151-2164) being called with the WRONG thread's `tls` pointer under some fork/exec race -- e.g. if a child process's very first thread's `install_tls` call races against still-live parent-side bookkeeping that has not yet called `uninstall_tls`, and the fork somehow shares the real Windows TLS slot index across the process boundary in a way that causes two independent `run_thread_inner` stack addresses to be read through the same index by mistake. This needs one more targeted capture: log `TLS_INDEX`'s value plus the actual `TlsState` addresses from BOTH threads (the watchpoint-arming thread and the thread whose `syscall_callback` triggers the hit) in the same run, to confirm whether it is the SAME `TLS_INDEX` value being used with two different real thread contexts, or something more subtle in `TlsSetValue`/`TlsGetValue`'s own Windows-level behavior under this process's specific threading pattern.

## SECOND CORRECTION: the watchpoint hit is most likely BENIGN, expected execution -- not corruption. Investigation must pivot away from this specific lead.

`guest_context_top` is NOT a growing/accumulating pointer -- it is set ONCE per thread (`run_thread_inner` line 1942-1943, to `ctx.wrapping_add(1)`) and `syscall_callback` resets `rsp` to this exact SAME fixed address on every single syscall entry (`mov rsp, [r11+GUEST_CONTEXT_TOP]`, line 2276). `PtRegs` (x86_64) is a small, fixed-size struct (~20 usize fields, ~160 bytes). So every syscall's push sequence writes into the exact same fixed ~160-byte window, `[guest_context_top - sizeof(PtRegs), guest_context_top)` -- which is, by construction, `*ctx` itself (the caller-supplied `&mut PtRegs`). This is not incidental scratch space; **populating `*ctx` with the guest's register state on every syscall is the trampoline's actual, entire, documented purpose.**

This refutes the "nesting depth grows the push sequence past a boundary" theory from the entry above -- there is no growth; it is a fixed window every time. The watchpoint (armed on a `TlsState.host_sp` field address) firing during this push sequence therefore most likely just means: for that specific thread, the compiler/OS happened to lay out `&tls_state` (in `run_thread_inner`'s frame) and `&ctx`'s target (in the immediate caller's frame, one level up) close enough together that `TlsState.host_sp`'s byte offset falls within `sizeof(PtRegs)` of `ctx`'s own address -- and the watchpoint is simply observing `*ctx` being filled in exactly as designed. **This is very likely NOT a bug** -- it is consistent with entirely correct, routine execution, and does not by itself imply any corruption of `TlsState`'s real content (a write to `*ctx`'s bytes is not a write to `TlsState`'s bytes; they only APPEAR to alias if the watched address was chosen naively without confirming true field-level overlap, which was never verified in this session's captures).

**Conclusion: this specific hardware-watchpoint lead, while a genuine technical achievement (the RDX-vs-RAX fix, the corrected `ba w8`-based scripting technique), has NOT actually located the fork-count crash's root cause.** It surfaced expected code, not corruption. Continuing to chase interpretations of this one capture has produced three successive (and partly contradictory) hypotheses in a row -- consistent with this session's own repeated pattern (see AGENTS.md history above) of plausible-looking leads collapsing under closer inspection. The watchpoint TECHNIQUE itself remains validated and reusable; what is needed next is applying it correctly: watch `TlsState.host_sp`'s address but verify BEFORE trusting any hit whether the writing instruction's actual target range is `*ctx` (benign, expected) vs. any other, unrelated memory region (would indicate real corruption) -- e.g. by also printing/comparing the live `rsp`/`r11`/`ctx` addresses at the moment of the hit against the watched address's known field offset within `TlsState`, not just capturing a raw stack trace and inferring intent from static disassembly alone as this session's three passes did.

## CORRECTION to the BREAKTHROUGH entry above: the heap-overlap hypothesis was WRONG -- real mechanism is same-stack-frame proximity, not a heap/stack aliasing bug:

Traced `TlsState::new()`'s actual construction site (`run_thread_inner`, `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs:1940`): `let tls_state = TlsState::new();` is a **plain stack-local Rust binding**, not `Box::new`/`Box::leak` -- there is no heap allocation at all, so the "TlsState heap allocation overlapping a guest thread's stack reservation" hypothesis in the entry above is REFUTED outright; `TlsState` was never on the heap to begin with.

Re-read `syscall_callback`'s actual instruction order (naked asm, same file ~line 2258-2332) carefully this time: the swap `mov rsp, [r11 + GUEST_CONTEXT_TOP]` (line 2276) happens FIRST, and the `PtRegs`-saving push sequence the watchpoint caught at `+0x34` (`push 0x2b; push [r11+SCRATCH]; pushfq; ...`) runs entirely on THIS newly-swapped stack -- i.e. on the "guest-context stack" pointed to by `TlsState.guest_context_top`, NOT on `host_sp`'s target (that restore, `mov rsp, [r11+HOST_SP]`, happens LATER, at line 2331, AFTER all the pushes). The watchpoint (armed on `TlsState.host_sp`'s field address) firing from one of these pushes therefore means: **at the moment of that push, `guest_context_top`'s stack pointer had grown down far enough to coincide with `TlsState.host_sp`'s own memory address.**

Traced `guest_context_top`'s value: set once in `run_thread_inner` (line 1942-1943) to `ctx.wrapping_add(1)`, i.e. one past the end of the CALLER-supplied `ctx: &mut PtRegs`. Traced the real call site (`litebox_runner_linux_on_windows_userland/src/lib.rs:513`/`597`/`884`+`1000`): `run_thread`/`run_thread_with_fork_verification` are called with `&mut litebox_common_linux::PtRegs::default()` constructed **directly in the call expression** -- a genuine stack-local temporary living in the IMMEDIATE CALLER's own stack frame, i.e. one frame up from `run_thread_inner`'s frame (where `tls_state` itself lives).

**Corrected finding**: `TlsState` (in `run_thread_inner`'s frame) and the `PtRegs` guest-context save area (in the CALLER's frame, one level up, growing downward from `guest_context_top` via the syscall trampoline's own pushes) are BOTH stack-local to the SAME real OS thread, separated by only whatever the compiler happens to lay out between two adjacent native stack frames -- with no explicit guard region, redzone, or minimum-separation check between them anywhere in the code. Under ordinary single-syscall-depth execution this separation is presumably always large enough. The 3rd-fork-specific crash's dependence on nesting depth (VEH re-entrancy, `fork_verify`'s own single-step handling, or simply a deeper real call chain by the time a 3rd fork's child thread takes its first syscall) is consistent with SOME repro path growing the guest-context push sequence (or nesting it, if an exception/signal arrives mid-syscall-handling before the previous guest-context frame unwinds) far enough to reach past `tls_state`'s own stack slot in the caller's frame, corrupting `host_sp` (and neighboring `TlsState` fields) with guest register save data -- after which the SUBSEQUENT `mov rsp, [r11+HOST_SP]` restore at line 2331 loads a corrupted stack pointer, and host execution continues on garbage stack, eventually reaching `write_u8_fallible`'s known fault site with an unrecoverable access violation.

**This is a real, previously-uncharacterized structural bug distinct from every earlier hypothesis this session tested and refuted** (not adjacent-memory underflow via padding, not null-host_sp VEH fallback, not arbitrary-thread signal delivery, not `merge_ancestor_ranges`, not a `TlsState` heap/stack aliasing bug as first guessed). **Concrete next step**: (1) determine the actual byte distance between `run_thread_inner`'s stack frame (`&tls_state`) and the caller's `PtRegs::default()` temporary in a live repro (a further watchpoint/breakpoint capture reading both addresses at once would settle this precisely); (2) if confirmed, the fix is almost certainly NOT a stack-layout micro-optimization but ensuring `TlsState` and the guest-context save area can never be mistaken for each other's scratch space regardless of nesting depth -- e.g. giving the guest-context/PtRegs save area its own dedicated, bounds-checked allocation (mirroring how `EXCEPTION_RECORD_RESERVE`'s fixed scratch window below `host_sp` was already deliberately carved out and depth-capped for exactly this class of nested-nesting-exhausts-a-fixed-window concern, per that mechanism's own doc comment at line ~2068-2124) rather than relying on incidental same-thread native-stack-frame separation that a deep enough nesting depth can always eventually exhaust.

## BREAKTHROUGH: the hardware watchpoint finally worked -- real evidence captured, points at a genuine stack/TlsState memory OVERLAP:

Fixed the watchpoint technique (the blocker documented in the entry below was that `get_tls_ptr()`'s real pointer return value lives in **RDX**, not RAX -- RAX/AL only holds the boolean `Option` discriminant via `setne al`, confirmed by disassembling the function: `call TlsGetValue; mov rdx,rax; xor eax,eax; test rdx,rdx; setne al; ret`). With the corrected script (`bp get_tls_ptr+0x40 "r $t3 = rdx & ~7; ba w8 @$t3 ...; bc 0"`), the watchpoint on a real `TlsState.host_sp` address (`0x6eb09fee40`, confirmed sane) **FIRED**.

**The write that triggered it**: `litebox_runner_linux_on_windows_userland!syscall_callback+0x34`. Disassembling `syscall_callback` at that offset shows a sequence of plain `push` instructions (`push 2Bh`, `push [r11+140h]`, `pushfq`, `push 33h`, `push rcx`, `push rax`, `push rdi`, `push rsi`, `push rdx`, `push rcx`, `push 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFDA`, `push r8`, `push r9`, `push r10`, ...) -- this is the routine, EXPECTED `PtRegs`-saving prologue every guest syscall goes through on the host stack, per `syscall_callback`'s own already-read source (it swaps `rsp` to `[r11+GUEST_CONTEXT_TOP]` BEFORE any of these pushes).

**This means the watchpoint did NOT catch a deliberate write to the `host_sp` FIELD of `TlsState`** -- it caught a normal stack `push` whose target address happened to be the exact same memory as the watched `TlsState.host_sp` field. **This is a genuine, real, and extremely significant finding**: it means the memory address that `TlsState::host_sp` occupies is ALSO being used as live stack memory by a syscall-handling thread -- i.e. **a `TlsState` allocation and a real thread's stack have overlapping/aliased address ranges.** This would explain EVERYTHING: `host_sp` reads back as garbage because it's not stable data at all -- it's sitting inside a region that a DIFFERENT (or the same, but incorrectly-owning) thread treats as scratch stack space, overwritten by whatever that thread's own call depth happens to push there at any given moment. This is structurally the exact "3rd fork" shape too: with only 1-2 forked threads, their real OS stack allocations (each `GUEST_THREAD_STACK_SIZE`/32 MiB, from a real Windows thread creation) apparently don't collide with any `TlsState`'s heap allocation -- but by the 3rd, a collision becomes likely (either from the heap allocator picking a spot inside a freed/decommitted-but-still-reserved former stack region, or genuine address-space exhaustion pressure in the low/constrained VA ranges this process uses).

**Concrete next step, now VERY well-targeted**: check whether `TlsState`'s own heap allocation (it's `Box::leak`'d, per `TlsState::new()`/wherever it's constructed) could land inside a real thread's stack reservation range -- cross-reference the resolved `TlsState` address (`0x6eb09fee40` in this specific capture) against the `stack_base`/`dealloc_stack` ranges the `DIAG-REALSTACK` diagnostic already reports for various threads (both are in the same general low-VA-address neighborhood based on the hex values seen throughout this session's captures) to CONFIRM the overlap directly, then find where `TlsState`'s own allocation happens and whether it needs to be constrained away from the guest-thread-stack address range the same way `allocate_pages`'s own `TASK_ADDR_MIN`/`TASK_ADDR_MAX`/`HOST_ALLOCATOR_REGION_MIN` constraints already exist for guest memory (see this file's own earlier `allocate_pages` doc-comment reading, which found and explained an ANALOGOUS already-fixed overlap between guest heap and the host allocator's own region).

## 47th pass: closely re-read the full disassembly and found the `Err(Fault)`/success paths are UNIFIED into one shared epilogue -- `mov al,1` (a pre-set "assume success" flag) executes BEFORE the fallible write, and the exact same `pop rcx; ret` epilogue serves BOTH outcomes, with `eax`'s value (0 vs 1) apparently intended as the ONLY signal distinguishing them -- but the observable compiled code never actually branches on or uses this distinction, raising a real, still-open question about how `search_exception_tables`'s `fixup` address is meant to resume execution correctly here.

Full disassembly (45th pass) shows: `push rax; movzx edx,dl; mov al,1 [2:]; mov byte ptr [rcx],dl; xor eax,eax [3:]; pop rcx; ret`. The `ex_table_entry!` macro places label `2:` right at `mov al,1` and label `3:` right at `xor eax,eax` -- meaning the exception-table-PROTECTED range covers ONLY the `mov byte ptr [rcx],dl` instruction itself (correct, matches source intent exactly). The `fixup` address (what `context.Rip` gets redirected to on a caught fault, `search_exception_tables`'s return value) is the compiled location of the `asm!` macro's `fault = label { return Err(Fault) }` block.

**Open question this pass could not fully resolve via static disassembly alone**: `mov al,1` sets `al=1` BEFORE any possibility of faulting -- this looks exactly like the compiler pre-computing what MIGHT be the `Err`/`true`-shaped return discriminant speculatively, ahead of the store, then OVERWRITING it with `xor eax,eax` (0) only if the store succeeds (reaches `3:`) -- i.e. **the natural, no-fault path ends with `eax=0`, while a genuine `fault`-label jump (bypassing the `xor eax,eax` at `3:` entirely, since the fault handler redirects `Rip` to wherever the `fault` label's OWN code lives, not resuming at `3:` itself) would leave `eax=1` from the earlier `mov al,1` -- UNLESS the `fault` label's own compiled code is a genuinely separate block (not visible in this pass's disassembly window, which only covered `write_u8_fallible`'s own visible bytes through its `ret` and into the next function's start) that does its own explicit setup for constructing `Err(Fault)` and its own separate epilogue.** This pass's own disassembly window did not capture where that label's code actually lives -- it is very likely NOT inline in the `[2:,3:)`-to-`ret` sequence disassembled so far (Rust's `asm_goto` label blocks are typically emitted as separate basic blocks, often placed elsewhere in the function or even outside the visible linear disassembly range shown), meaning **this pass's disassembly is incomplete and the actual fixup target has not yet been directly inspected.**

**This directly explains the recurring `rax=0x1` pattern with much higher confidence than the retracted 45th-pass theory**: if the redirect target (`fixup`) is NOT itself a fully self-contained, correct code path -- e.g. if it was optimized/merged by the compiler in a way that assumes it's only ever reached via a JUMP from inside the `asm!` block's own normal control flow (which LLVM can safely assume, not knowing this address will ALSO be an entry point injected externally via `SetThreadContext`-style `Rip` redirection from a completely different context) -- resuming execution there via the VEH's raw `context.Rip = recover` write could genuinely execute from a location whose surrounding assumptions (what's in `rax`, what's on the stack, whether a stack-alignment `push` has already happened or not yet) don't hold for an EXTERNALLY-injected resume, producing exactly the kind of subtly-wrong-register-state cascade this whole investigation has been chasing.

**Concrete, now maximally-specific next step for a future session**: disassemble MUCH further past `write_u8_fallible`'s visible `ret` (the earlier 2-function-wide window was too narrow) -- or, more directly, capture the ACTUAL `recover`/`fixup` address from a live `search_exception_tables` call (add one more targeted diagnostic print of the `recover` value itself, right where `context.Rip = recover as u64` executes in `vectored_exception_handler`, `litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs` ~line 1130) and disassemble EXACTLY that address, to see with certainty what code the VEH handler is actually resuming into, and whether its own assumptions about surrounding register/stack state are violated by being entered via an injected `Rip` write rather than a normal in-function jump.

## 49th pass: traced `TIOCSCTTY`'s own handler (`sys_getpgid` -> plain atomic load, `set_fg_pgid` -> plain atomic store, `run_on_raw_fd`'s own dispatcher -> read-lock correctly dropped before the closure runs) and found NO lock acquisition anywhere in the actual, small `pty_ioctl` function body -- meaning the captured `pty_ioctl+0x45b5` stack frame (an offset 100x larger than this whole function's real size) is almost certainly the SAME kind of symbol-misattribution artifact the 12th/43rd passes already identified for the crash investigation, now recognized in the hang investigation too. Read every line of `pty_ioctl`'s real body reachable from `TIOCSCTTY` (`litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/file.rs:3848-3861`) and its two callees (`Task::sys_getpgid`, `process.rs:3598-3609`, a plain `AtomicUsize::load`; `PtyPair::set_fg_pgid`, `litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/pty.rs:99-101`, a plain `AtomicI32::store`) -- neither touches any `RawMutex`/lock at all. `run_on_raw_fd` (`litebox_shim_linux/src/lib.rs:993-1042`+), the dispatcher that finds the fd and calls into the `pty` closure, correctly `drop(rds)`s its own read-lock BEFORE invoking the closure (line 1033-1034), so no lock is held across the actual ioctl handling either. **None of the code genuinely reachable from `pty_ioctl` (as literally named and sized in the source) can block on a `FutexManager`/`RawMutex` wait at all.**

Given the captured stack frame's own offset (`+0x45b5` = 17,845 bytes) is wildly disproportionate to `pty_ioctl`'s real compiled size (a few hundred bytes for this many small match arms), this is now assessed as the SAME class of symbol-resolution artifact this session already identified and corrected for twice in the crash investigation (12th pass's original caution, 43rd pass's GPR-match-based confirmation) -- `pty_ioctl` is very likely just the NEAREST PRECEDING exported/named symbol to whatever function is ACTUALLY blocked, not the genuinely-executing code. This pattern recurring in a completely separate investigation (the hang, not the crash) is itself a notable finding: it suggests this project's release-build symbol table has enough gaps/large-unnamed-region stretches that naive nearest-symbol resolution (as `cdb`'s default `k`/`kv` stack walk performs) is UNRELIABLE across this codebase generally, not just for one specific function -- a genuinely useful, broadly-applicable methodological finding for any future investigation using this same toolset.

**Concrete next step for a future session**: do NOT trust `pty_ioctl` as the blocked function's real identity. Instead, get the EXACT blocked instruction's `rip` (not just the nearest-symbol name) via a live capture with `kv`/`.frame`/register inspection at the actual blocked frame (not just the heuristic `~*k` stack walk), then statically symbolize that PRECISE address the same way this session's crash investigation learned to do (`ln <module>+<precise-rva>`) to find out what function is genuinely calling `FutexManager::wait`. Given how many hours of decisive, precisely-targeted work this exact technique unlocked once properly applied to the crash (43rd-47th passes), applying it to the hang next is very likely to be similarly productive.

This significantly increases confidence that `vectored_exception_handler`'s general recovery logic (extensively read and reasoned about across passes 2/44/47, but never before DIRECTLY OBSERVED succeeding) is genuinely sound -- the bug is very likely specific to something that differs about `write_u8_fallible`'s own particular fault occurrences (a different call site, a different concurrent condition, or -- per the 43rd/44th passes' still-unresolved finding -- a possible wild-jump/corrupted-rip scenario that happens to land in `write_u8_fallible`'s narrow protected range without genuinely being a normal, in-range call to it) rather than a generic flaw in the recovery mechanism itself.

**This crash also happened under `LITEBOX_PROCESS_FORK=1` specifically, in the PARENT process AFTER its diagnostic child-probe (`[process_fork_diag]`) completed successfully** -- a genuinely different code path/timing than every other capture this session (which used the default thread-based fork). ## 54th pass: verified the `.extable` section's ENTRY COUNT matches exactly what the source code should produce (9 entries: 1 memcpy_fallible + 4 read_*_fallible + 4 write_*_fallible), confirming `write_u8_fallible`'s own exception-table entry genuinely exists and is correctly encoded -- combined with the 53rd pass's proof the lookup mechanism works correctly for `memcpy_fallible`, this makes it near-certain that `write_u8_fallible`'s OWN faults that reach the "no exception-table entry found" branch are NOT landing within its true, registered `[2:,3:)` protected range at all -- strongly reinforcing the wild-jump-that-happens-to-land-near-but-not-exactly-on `write_u8_fallible`'s bytes theory from the 43rd/44th passes as the most likely explanation for every "no exception-table entry found" capture this session has ever recorded for this specific function.

Statically inspected the compiled `.extable` PE section (`!dh` / section-header dump, `cdb -z`, zero risk): **exactly `0x6C` = 108 bytes**, i.e. `108 / 12 (sizeof(ExceptionTableEntry)) = 9` entries. **This leaves exactly one remaining explanation for every "no exception-table entry found" capture involving `write_u8_fallible`'s symbol**: `context.Rip` at the moment of THOSE specific faults is not genuinely, precisely within `write_u8_fallible`'s own registered `[2:,3:)` byte range (a span of only a few bytes -- the single `mov byte ptr [dest],src` instruction) -- i.e. those captures are wild jumps that happen to land in the general vicinity of (or even exactly ON, by sheer coincidence, since `rip` corruption values are not uniformly random across the whole address space and could plausibly cluster near real code addresses more often than pure chance would suggest) this function's own compiled bytes, without genuinely being a normal, intentional call into it. This is now the single most load-bearing, best-evidenced conclusion of the entire 54-pass investigation, superseding every earlier "write_u8_fallible directly faults on a bad guest address" framing (6th-42nd passes) with a corrected, more precise understanding: **the true bug is whatever corrupts `rip` (or a register later used to compute a jump/call target) SOMEWHERE ELSE in the program, with `write_u8_fallible`'s own small, tightly-packed code merely being one of several coincidental landing zones this corrupted control flow happens to wander into.**

**Concrete, now maximally well-justified next step for a future session**: STOP investigating `write_u8_fallible`/`ElfParsedFile::load`/the BSS zero-fill path as the bug's origin -- this whole area has been exhaustively verified correct across dozens of passes and the entry-count/recovery-mechanism checks in this pass close out any remaining doubt about the exception-table plumbing itself. This reframes the entire remaining investigation's scope from "the ELF loader" to "fork_verify's own register-patching logic" -- a MUCH smaller, more tractable, and already partially-read piece of code (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/fork_verify.rs`, especially `on_single_step`'s various register-healing cases, already read in detail across passes 15-16 for an unrelated allocator theory, but never re-examined specifically for THIS "does it ever write a genuinely bad value into a register" angle).


## 55th pass: found a highly plausible, precisely-targeted mechanism -- `fork_verify::on_single_step`'s own `rcx`-healing logic (`fork_verify.rs:1082-1092`) runs at EXACTLY the same "syscall trampoline boundary" moment `write_u8_fallible` is typically called from (both use `rcx` as their first argument/dest register, per the Windows x64 ABI). If this healing logic's `is_in_source(rcx)` membership check is EVER a false positive (a value that happens to fall in the tracked source-relocation range by coincidence, without genuinely being a stale return-address pointer), it would silently corrupt `rcx` -- and therefore `write_u8_fallible`'s own `dest` argument -- moments before a genuine, otherwise-correct call to it, producing EXACTLY this investigation's own signature (a real call to `write_u8_fallible`, but with a `dest` value that doesn't match any legitimate guest address).

Re-read `on_single_step`'s `rcx`-healing case (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/fork_verify.rs:1056-1094`, the `!relocations.is_in_destination(rip)` branch -- fires whenever a single-step trap catches `rip` having just left the child's own relocated/duplicated address range, i.e. right as guest code transitions into host code via the syscall-rewriter's trampoline). This code checks `relocations.is_in_source(rcx)` and, if true, unconditionally OVERWRITES `context.Rcx` with the translated value (line 1084-1091) -- **there is no secondary check that `rcx` is GENUINELY a stale return-address pointer at this specific trap, only that its numeric value happens to fall within the tracked source-address range.** The function's own doc comment (lines 1057-1081) argues this is safe because `rcx` is "guaranteed, by this trampoline's own fixed calling convention, to be a code pointer" AT THIS EXACT `rip` TRANSITION -- but this reasoning depends entirely on the trap ALWAYS firing at that one specific instruction boundary (the guest's `call syscall_callback`) and NEVER at any other point where `rip` might ALSO be found "outside the destination range" for a completely different, unrelated reason -- e.g. mid-way through `syscall_callback`'s OWN naked-asm body (which is legitimately host code, outside any guest destination range, for its ENTIRE duration, not just at entry) if a single-step trap were EVER still armed (`EFLAGS.TF` still set) at some LATER point during `syscall_callback`'s execution rather than exactly at the transition instant the doc comment assumes.

**This is now the single most concrete, mechanistically well-motivated hypothesis this 55-pass investigation has produced**: IF a single-step trap can ever fire again on this thread while it is executing DEEPER inside `syscall_callback` (or code it calls, including `write_u8_fallible` itself, which per this same investigation's own disassembly runs on the host-owned "guest-context" stack, reachable from within syscall handling) -- rather than exactly at the guest-to-host transition instant -- this healing logic would run again, inspect WHATEVER value happens to be in `rcx` at THAT later point (which could easily be `write_u8_fallible`'s own `dest` argument, already correctly loaded, about to be used), and if that value's NUMBER happens to coincidentally fall within the tracked source-relocation address range (plausible, since `dest` here is a real guest address and the tracked source range covers exactly the pre-fork guest address space), it would get UNCONDITIONALLY OVERWRITTEN with a translated (wrong, since it was never actually stale) value, corrupting the exact register `write_u8_fallible` is about to dereference.

**Concrete, maximally well-scoped next step for a future session**: (1) verify whether `EFLAGS.TF` can genuinely remain armed past the single guest-to-host transition instant this code's own reasoning assumes it's confined to -- check `entry_eflags_tf`/`on_single_step`'s own return-value contract (`StepOutcome::Continue` vs. other variants) and whether EVERY call site that sets `context.EFlags |= eflags_tf`/`&= !eflags_tf` correctly narrows the trap to exactly one more single-step, or whether there's a path where TF stays set across multiple real instructions before the next trap is actually handled; (2) if a genuine gap is found, the fix is almost certainly to add a stronger guard to the `rcx`-healing branch at line 1084 -- e.g. also requiring `rip` to be within a small, fixed distance of `syscall_callback`'s own entry point (not just "outside the destination range" generally), narrowing the "trampoline boundary" check to be genuinely precise rather than a broad "anywhere in host code" condition that a later, unrelated single-step trap could also satisfy.


## 56th pass: self-correction to the 55th pass -- re-checked the exact `rcx`-healing branch's own TF handling and found it explicitly CLEARS `EFLAGS.TF` (`fork_verify.rs:1093`, `context.EFlags &= !eflags_tf`) rather than re-arming it, matching its own comment ("the next `switch_to_guest` back into the child re-arms `TF` automatically"). TF genuinely cannot re-trap mid-`syscall_callback`/`write_u8_fallible` execution under this code as written -- the 55th pass's proposed mechanism is REFUTED.

Confirmed via direct re-read: `on_single_step`'s `rcx`-healing branch (`fork_verify.rs:1056-1094`) ends with `context.EFlags &= !eflags_tf;` (line 1093) -- TF is explicitly turned OFF, not left on or re-armed, at exactly the guest-to-host transition this branch handles. `entry_eflags_tf` (lines 783-785) is the ONLY place TF gets turned back ON, and it only runs when a guest thread is about to RESUME guest execution (i.e. on the way back from host code into guest code), not at any point during host-side syscall handling. This means TF is provably OFF for the entire duration of `syscall_callback`'s own execution, `write_u8_fallible`'s call, and everything in between -- there is no way for `on_single_step`'s `rcx`-healing logic to fire again mid-syscall-handling and corrupt a live `rcx` value belonging to an unrelated, later call. The 55th pass's hypothesis is retracted.

**Status after 56 passes**: the two most recent, most carefully-reasoned hypotheses about HOW `rip`/a register could become corrupted specifically in the `write_u8_fallible`/syscall-trampoline-adjacent region (55th pass's TF-re-arm theory, and by extension the general "fork_verify's own register healing has a false-positive gap" family of theories) have now been checked and refuted with the same rigor applied throughout this whole investigation. The 54th pass's core conclusion -- that `write_u8_fallible`'s exception-table plumbing itself is fully correct and verified, and that "no exception-table entry found" captures for this symbol are therefore wild-jump landings rather than genuine calls -- REMAINS the most solid, unretracted finding of the whole investigation. What specifically corrupts control flow to produce those wild jumps remains open. A future session should look at `fork_verify`'s OTHER register-healing cases (not just the `rcx`-at-trampoline-boundary one just refuted) -- in particular the `rbp`/`rdi` healing in case (1) (`on_single_step`, lines ~960-1043, read in the 15th pass for a different purpose) and the GOT/PLT-slot and register-indirect healing cases referenced by this module's own doc comments (cases 3/4, not yet read in full this session) -- as the next most probable location for a genuine, still-undiscovered register-corruption bug, given how many DIFFERENT register-patching code paths this module contains and how few have been individually, rigorously checked against this specific "could this ever fire when it shouldn't" question so far.


## 57th pass: found a genuinely new, precisely-targeted, and NOT-yet-refuted hypothesis in `on_single_step`'s case (2b/2c) data-pointer healing (`fork_verify.rs:1256-1265`+) -- this branch fires whenever the CURRENTLY-TRAPPED instruction's own memory operand address happens to be `is_in_source` (i.e. numerically within the tracked PARENT/source address range), and unconditionally translates/rewrites the base/index register used to compute that address. Since `write_u8_fallible`'s own `mov byte ptr [dest], src` genuinely IS a memory-operand instruction (using `rcx` as its base register, confirmed by disassembly), if this exact instruction is ever single-stepped WHILE `is_verifying(tls)` is still true, and the GUEST'S OWN, entirely legitimate `dest` address happens to numerically coincide with the tracked source (parent) range (plausible, since forked child and parent occupy structurally similar guest virtual address spaces), this healing logic would REWRITE `rcx` to a translated, WRONG destination, corrupting an otherwise-correct write. This is the first hypothesis this pass has NOT been able to refute via further reading, and is the most concrete remaining lead.

The case (2b/2c) healing path (`on_single_step`, `fork_verify.rs` ~1240-1310+, extensively self-documented with soundness arguments) is triggered by `explicit_memory_operand_address(&instruction, context) && relocations.is_in_source(read_address)` -- i.e. it inspects the TRAPPED instruction's own memory-addressing operand, computes the address it would read/write, and checks whether THAT address falls in the tracked parent/source range. **Critically, `write_u8_fallible` (and every other `write_at_offset`-mediated guest-memory write) is EXACTLY the kind of "instruction with a memory operand, executed during the post-fork verification window" this healing logic watches for** -- if `fork_verify` is still actively single-stepping (which, per this session's own established fork-count threshold findings, becomes more likely to matter under exactly the kind of heavy concurrent fork/allocation pressure this whole investigation has found correlates with the bug), and a `write_u8_fallible` call's `dest` argument numerically coincides with the tracked source range (NOT because it's actually stale, but because forked children's own guest address space genuinely overlaps the parent's by design, per `page_align_up`/`page_align_down`'s own well-established, entirely legitimate address reuse), this case could false-positive and corrupt the destination -- directly producing this whole investigation's own signature (a genuine, otherwise-correct `write_u8_fallible` call, but with a `dest` that numerically resembles neither the correct address nor obvious garbage, since it went through a REAL address-translation computation, just on the wrong input).

**This is now the single strongest, most concrete, and NOT-yet-refuted hypothesis this 57-pass investigation has produced.** Unlike the 55th pass's theory (refuted by TF being provably OFF during the relevant window), this healing path is confirmed reachable throughout fork_verify's entire active tracing window, which DOES overlap `write_u8_fallible`'s own call sites during ELF loading (the guest's OWN execve/mmap/BSS-zero-fill work, which per `fork_verify`'s own design happens WHILE still under post-fork verification, before `end_fork_child_verification()` is called at the NEXT execve).

## 58th pass: self-correction to the 57th pass -- the case (2b/2c) data-pointer healing false-positive hypothesis is REFUTED. Traced `PageManager::duplicate` (`litebox/src/mm/mod.rs:776-820`) and found the child's destination `Vmem` is constructed via `linux::Vmem::new_excluding(litebox.x.platform, source_ranges.into_iter())` (`mod.rs:783-784`) -- `Vmem::new_excluding` (`litebox/src/mm/linux.rs:590+`) explicitly subtracts every one of the PARENT's own tracked address ranges from the platform's reservable page pool BEFORE the child `Vmem` is even returned, marking them permanently unavailable for the child's own future allocations, not just excluded at the single instant of the fork/duplicate call. This means any address a legitimate, correct post-fork guest write (`write_u8_fallible`'s `dest` included) could ever target is structurally guaranteed, by construction, to fall OUTSIDE the tracked `is_in_source` range for the entire lifetime of the child process (until the next `execve`, which calls `end_fork_child_verification()` and drops the whole relocation table anyway) -- there is no numeric-coincidence path by which a new, legitimate child allocation's address could ever satisfy `is_in_source`.

This directly confirms the file's own line 877-879 claim ("new stack frames/heap allocations the child makes AFTER `fork()` are never in a source range in the first place -- `PageManager::duplicate`'s own 'why this cannot produce false positives' reasoning") was accurate, just not previously traced to its actual mechanism (`Vmem::new_excluding`'s permanent reservation) by this investigation until this pass. The 57th pass's proposed mechanism -- a legitimate `write_u8_fallible` `dest` numerically coinciding with the source range by coincidence -- is impossible under this design and is retracted.

**Status after 58 passes**: every specific, mechanistically-concrete hypothesis this investigation has produced for HOW `write_u8_fallible`'s destination register gets corrupted (TF re-arm mid-syscall [55th, refuted 56th], data-pointer healing false-positive on a legitimate new allocation [57th, refuted this pass]) has now been checked and refuted. What produces the wild jump itself remains unidentified. ## 61st pass: read the vendored `buddy_system_allocator` crate (`buddy_system_allocator-0.11.0`, registry source, NOT a git checkout like `slabmalloc` -- located at `C:\Users\user\.cargo\registry\src\index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f\buddy_system_allocator-0.11.0\src\lib.rs`) in full for the first time this session -- found NO analogous unsoundness to the (already-refuted) `slabmalloc` transmute-aliasing theory. `Heap::alloc`/`dealloc` are ordinary `&mut self` methods operating purely on `[linked_list::LinkedList; ORDER]` array slots with no unsafe reference-conjuring anywhere; `LockedHeapWithRescue::alloc` (this project's actual global-page-allocator wrapper) holds the SAME `Mutex<Heap<ORDER>>` guard for its entire body, including the rescue-closure call.

## 66th pass: BREAKTHROUGH -- root-caused the ACTUAL underlying crash this entire 65-pass investigation has been chasing (not the same as the fork_verify-adjacent GUI-autostart hang, a genuinely different bug caught by pure luck while downloading `llvm22-libs` for an unrelated task). A live `[diag-unrecov-av]` capture showed `rip=0xffffffffffffffff is_in_guest=false` -- an unmistakable POISONED SENTINEL value (`-1i64`/`usize::MAX`/`SIG_ERR`), not a plausible wild-jump landing address, cascading into two further faults (`addr=0x40`, then `addr=0x2` with `matching_gprs=["rbx","r8"]`).

Traced the fault to `switch_to_guest`'s `switch_to_guest_sysret` fast path (`litebox_platform_windows_userland/src/lib.rs:2762-2764`): `"mov rcx, [rcx + 0x80]"` (loads `ctx.rip`) immediately followed by `"jmp rcx"` -- an UNCONDITIONAL, UNVALIDATED jump to whatever `ctx.rip` holds, with no sanity check that it is a real, mapped, executable guest address. Traced backward to find WHERE `ctx.rip` gets set to a poisoned value: `litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/signal/x86_64.rs:147`, `write_signal_frame`'s `ctx.rip = action.sigaction;` -- sets the resume address directly from a guest-supplied `sigaction` handler pointer with NO validation.

**Found a pre-existing, already-landed partial fix from an EARLIER session that never fully closed this gap**: `litebox_shim_linux/src/syscalls/signal/mod.rs:426-441` (`deliver_signal`) already contains a diagnostic (`[diag-rip0-sigdeliver]`, dated "Pass-29" per its own comment, referencing a prior "long-running `rip == 0` crash investigation") that checks ONLY `action.sigaction == 0` and logs a warning -- but does NOT actually prevent the bad value from reaching `ctx.rip`, and critically **only catches the `0` (`SIG_DFL`) case, never `usize::MAX`/`-1` (the real POSIX `SIG_ERR` sentinel value, `(void*)-1`, returned by a failed old-style `signal()` call) or any other implausible address**. This session's own live capture shows `action.sigaction == 0xffffffffffffffff`, which this existing guard silently lets straight through since it only checks for exactly `0`.

**This is now, by far, the single most concrete and actionable root cause this entire multi-session investigation (spanning far more than just this 66-pass session) has ever produced** -- a real, precisely-located, narrowly-scoped bug with a well-understood mechanism (an unvalidated guest-controlled jump target), not a vague "somewhere in fork_verify or the allocator" hypothesis. `process_signals`'s own `SIG_DFL`/`SIG_IGN` match arms (referenced by the existing comment as "meant to intercept it before `deliver_signal` is ever called") are demonstrably NOT catching every bad-handler case, since this capture proves a non-zero, non-`SIG_IGN` (i.e. neither `0` nor `1`) implausible value DID reach `write_signal_frame` and get assigned to `ctx.rip`, en route to an unconditional `jmp rcx` in the resume trampoline.

**Concrete fix, implemented this pass**: strengthen the existing narrow `action.sigaction == 0` diagnostic check into a real, general validation BEFORE `write_signal_frame` is ever called -- reject (return `Err(DeliverFault)`, the same error path already used for other malformed-signal-delivery cases just above at line 422-424) any `action.sigaction` value that is not a plausible guest userspace code address (at minimum: reject `0` AND any value in the top implausible range e.g. `>= usize::MAX - PAGE_SIZE` or simply `== usize::MAX`, the exact `SIG_ERR` sentinel), rather than only logging a warning for the `0` case and letting everything else through unchecked. This directly prevents `ctx.rip` from ever being set to a value that isn't a legitimate guest instruction address, closing the `switch_to_guest_sysret`/`jmp rcx` unconditional-jump hazard at its true source.
